meta.blurb: King Edric's will names no heir, only a test: keep salt and ash at peace for a year and a day. His youngest daughter Sera sees that the letters pushing both sides toward war are forged. Who is writing them?
meta.bible: Edric Halvane: the old king of Haldmere, wise and tired, dies in beat one. Sera Halvane: his youngest child, seventeen, an archivist's apprentice, patient, observant, loves old records. Lysa Halvane: the eldest, twenty-four, commander of the Salt Guard, proud and honest, but stubborn. Torren Halvane: the middle child, twenty-one, charming and generous, always in debt. Dovan Karth: the Chancellor, keeper of the royal seal, smooth and polite, the villain. Oswin Pell: the Master Archivist, old and dry-humoured, Sera's teacher. Wick: a young royal courier, quick and brave. Kael Ashmoor: the lord of the Ash Hills, an ironmaster, blunt and fair. Brenna Ashmoor: Kael's daughter, a scout. Maren Tidewell: head of the salt guilds, calm and shrewd. Hob Fennick: a nervous copyist-clerk who forges for the Chancellor. Haldmere: the kingdom. Brinegate: the capital on the Greywater river. Saltmarch: the Salt Coast, flat shining salt pans by the sea. Cindermoor: the Ash Hills, dark volcanic hills with iron mines. Greywater: the river that divides the two lands. Weigh-Bridge: the border bridge where iron and salt are weighed; the Charter says weight for weight. Hall of Two Crowns: where the crowns are kept. Salt Crown: pale crystal. Ash Crown: dark volcanic glass. Salt Charter: the old agreement that fixed fair trade of iron for salt. Salt Guard: the army of the Salt Coast. Council: the new ruling table. Protector: the ruler in the Chancellor's plan. Edric ruled thirty-one years; his queen died when Sera was small. Inkwell: Pell's grey cat. Pell keeps white doves on the archive roof; they carry letters Karth cannot read. The deep vault: under the archive, where the oldest treaties are kept. Karth wore dark velvet. The false Charter clause: iron must pay a fee (levy) to the crown; the true clause says weight for weight, no fee either way. Clue: the forged papers have a small curl on the crossbar of the letter t (Fennick's habit). Pepper: Sera's grey mare. Captain Orla Vance: Lysa's second in command of the Salt Guard. Tam Greaves: the old keeper of the Weigh-Bridge scales, stubborn and fair. Edda: a young salt-raker of Saltmarch. Whitehaven: the town of the salt guild halls. Pan Harbour: the port of Saltmarch. Ironhold: Kael's hall in Cindermoor. Cinderford: the main town of Cindermoor. Deepwell: the great iron mine. Gilder Prowse: a moneylender in Brinegate whose ledger shows the Chancellor's silver. Lord Garrow Stane: a hot-headed Ash lord, loud but honest in the end. Mother Bessel: the palace cook. Dunstan Pike: a copyist who spreads rumours in spring. Tamsin Rook: the judge of the Court of Both Lands. Casimir Dorne: envoy from Varenna, a rich land across the sea. Open Book: the public record of Council orders kept in the archive. Scales of Two Crowns: great scales of iron and salt-glass cast at the Weigh-Bridge. Weigh-Day: the festival at summer's end, first held the year after the king's death. Palace Watch: the palace guards in grey cloaks, answering to the Chancellor. Marta: a Brinegate baker. Captain Orla Vance leads the Salt Guard detachment that takes Karth away. The Charter is about sixty years old. By the old law any Halvane may call the lords of both lands to the Hall of Two Crowns. The Council of Salt and Ash: three seats for the Salt Coast, three for the Ash Hills, a Halvane at its head without a vote, and the Archivist keeping the record. The king gave Pell a sealed envelope a week before he died; its last clause says the crown passes to whoever the people of salt and ash name as keeper of the peace. Edric's private letter, in a box beside the crowns: a crown that is given is only a hat, one earned is a bridge. Sera keeps a ring of iron and salt-glass and sets both crowns on the Council table. Timeline: the king dies in late summer; Karth falls in early autumn; the Scales are cast in autumn; the storm is in winter; the failed harvest in spring; the envoy and the Open Book in early summer; the trial in high summer; Weigh-Day at summer's end; the year and a day ends the next late summer. Voice and tone: tense, clear and clever, a political puzzle told step by step; nobody dies in battle; the threat of war is real but is stopped by truth, not swords.
chapters: A Table Instead of a Throne

beats.scene: An old king lies still in bed while his three children stand beside him
beats.summary: King Edric dies in his bed in Brinegate at midnight with his three children beside him.

beats.scene: Great bells ring above a foggy city of grey roofs and a wide river
beats.summary: The bells of Brinegate toll all night, and the people wake to learn that the old king is dead.

beats.scene: A pale crystal crown and a dark glass crown rest in a hall
beats.summary: The Salt Crown and the Ash Crown rest in the Hall of Two Crowns, joined long ago.

beats.scene: Three young people sit far apart at a very long table with cold food
beats.summary: The three Halvane children eat a cold supper in silence, each privately wondering who will rule.

beats.scene: A long line of mourners follows a coffin along a grey river
beats.summary: The funeral procession winds through Brinegate, with the Salt lords and the Ash lords walking on opposite sides.

beats.scene: A girl in a doorway sees a man in velvet gathering desk papers
beats.summary: At the funeral supper Sera slips away and finds Chancellor Karth gathering papers from the dead king's desk.

beats.scene: A smiling man in velvet carries a thick bundle of papers down a corridor
beats.summary: Karth explains that the kingdom's business cannot stop, then carries a bundle of papers toward Lysa's rooms.

beats.scene: A tall hall of listening nobles as the Chancellor unrolls a long scroll
beats.summary: The will is read: it names no heir, but the crown will go to whoever keeps salt and ash at peace for a year and a day.

beats.scene: A woman in armour strides down steps as a young man calls for horses
beats.summary: Lysa orders the Salt Guard to the border, and Torren rides off to win the Ash lords with feasts.

beats.scene: A girl sits alone at a bare desk by a single candle
beats.summary: Alone in her father's study, Sera decides to find out what was really promised between the two lands.

beats.scene: A girl climbs down a spiral stair into a vast archive of shelves
beats.summary: The next morning Sera goes down to the archive under the palace, where she has been an apprentice for two years.

beats.scene: An old man with a grey cat on his shoulder pours tea among scrolls
beats.summary: Master Pell, the old Archivist, greets her with tea and his cat Inkwell, and tells her that grief is best faced with work.

beats.scene: A girl and an old man bend over a will, tracing a line
beats.summary: Sera shows Pell how strangely the will is worded, and he says someone should read what was actually agreed.

beats.scene: An old man holds a lens over two samples of handwriting beside a lamp
beats.summary: Pell teaches her how to tell one scribe from another by the shape of a letter, the pressure of a pen and the habits of a hand.

beats.scene: An old man hands a small iron key across a cluttered desk
beats.summary: Pell gives Sera the key to the deep vault where the oldest treaties of Haldmere are kept.

beats.scene: A girl with a lamp walks down a cold stone stair to a door
beats.summary: Sera descends to the cold vault, unlocks the door and finds shelves of dusty parchment stretching into the dark.

beats.scene: Sera unrolls a cracked parchment under a lamp, covered in neat old script
beats.summary: Sera finds the original Salt Charter, which says iron and salt are traded weight for weight.

beats.scene: A girl reads aloud from a parchment while shadows move on the vault wall
beats.summary: The Charter tells how the first Halvane king ended the old wars, and it promises scales at the bridge and no fee either way.

beats.scene: A young courier with a muddy satchel bursts into the archive, grinning
beats.summary: Wick, a young royal courier, tumbles into the archive with a message for Pell and makes Sera laugh.

beats.scene: A courier whispers to a girl beside a tall shelf, glancing at the door
beats.summary: Wick tells Sera that the Chancellor has ordered every royal letter to be handed to him alone.

beats.scene: A herald nails a fresh notice to a post in a busy square
beats.summary: A herald nails a fresh copy of the Salt Charter to a post in Brinegate's market square, and the crowd gathers to read.

beats.scene: A girl in a crowd frowns at a notice, finger on one line
beats.summary: Sera reads the posted Charter and stops: one clause does not say what she saw in the vault.

beats.scene: Sera holds a posted notice next to an old parchment, comparing the lines
beats.summary: Back in the vault, she lays the notice beside the old Charter and finds the changed clause: iron must now pay a fee.

beats.scene: A girl bends over a notice with a lens, circling one word
beats.summary: The false clause uses the word levy, which the old scribes never wrote, and the new ink does not match.

beats.scene: Master Pell shakes his head gravely at a desk crowded with scrolls
beats.summary: Pell studies the two copies and agrees that someone has changed the Charter on purpose.

beats.scene: An old man sits very still, one hand on a grey cat, in lamplight
beats.summary: Pell warns that accusing the Chancellor without proof would be dangerous, because Karth holds the seal and the palace guards.

beats.scene: An old man points at an empty chair in the dim archive
beats.summary: Pell tells her how a clerk once accused a lord without proof and was sent away to a far post, never to be heard from again.

beats.scene: A girl writes quickly in a notebook, her lamp low
beats.summary: Sera decides to collect proof quietly and begins a secret notebook of every difference between the true Charter and the false one.

beats.scene: A girl slides a rolled parchment between dull ledgers on a high shelf
beats.summary: Sera hides the true Charter among boring tax records, and Pell says the best place to hide a thing is where nobody reads.

beats.scene: A girl walks past two guards in grey, carrying a stack of books
beats.summary: Sera walks through the palace as if nothing has happened, pretending to be only a grieving apprentice.

beats.scene: A muddy rider gasps out news to Sera and Pell at the archive door
beats.summary: A rider arrives from the border with news that the Salt Guard is stopping iron carts at the Weigh-Bridge.

beats.scene: A crowd shouts at a bridge as soldiers block iron carts
beats.summary: The Salt Guard demands the new fee from every iron cart, and drivers turn back with their loads.

beats.scene: A young man raises a cup at a long feast table among dark-clad lords
beats.summary: In Cindermoor, Torren spends lavishly on feasts for the Ash lords and promises everything to everyone.

beats.scene: A broad man crumples a letter in his fist in a smoky ironworks
beats.summary: Lord Kael Ashmoor receives a letter with Lysa's seal that insults the Ash Hills and answers with a threat to close the mines.

beats.scene: Torren shows a crumpled letter to Sera in a candlelit room
beats.summary: Torren returns to Brinegate and shows Sera Kael's furious reply, which threatens to close the mines.

beats.scene: A girl studies a letter beside her brother, one eyebrow raised
beats.summary: Sera says that Lysa would never write such an insult, and Torren shrugs that Lysa is proud.

beats.scene: Torren returns dusty and flushed from the road, speaking loudly to a crowd
beats.summary: At a palace supper Torren boasts that the Ash lords would crown him and divide the kingdom.

beats.scene: A single window glows late in a high tower above a sleeping city
beats.summary: Sera notices that the Chancellor's window burns every night, and couriers come and go in the dark.

beats.scene: A girl and an old man lean over a map by candlelight
beats.summary: Sera and Pell agree that someone must reach the bridge before the soldiers start fighting, and Pell is too old to ride.

beats.scene: A girl and a courier lead two horses through a grey dawn gate
beats.summary: Sera packs the Charter and her notes, and at dawn Wick waits with two horses at the palace gate.

beats.scene: Sera rides a horse beside Wick along a white salt road
beats.summary: Sera and Wick leave Brinegate and ride east along the white salt road toward the coast.

beats.scene: Workers rake white salt into mounds on a vast flat shimmering coast
beats.summary: Riding through Saltmarch, Sera sees the vast salt pans, flat and bright as a frozen lake.

beats.scene: A girl with a salt rake talks with Sera beside a glittering pan
beats.summary: A young salt-raker called Edda tells Sera that prices have doubled since the iron stopped and that families are going hungry.

beats.scene: A market with half-empty stalls and worried people
beats.summary: In a village market the stalls are bare, and people blame the Ash lords for the new fee.

beats.scene: A small inn with a glowing hearth and travellers in blue cloaks
beats.summary: At an inn that night an old woman says the Ash lords are about to attack, and the whole room nods.

beats.scene: A crier in a square holds a scroll and a crowd listens
beats.summary: In the morning a crier reads a proclamation about Ash treachery, and Sera notices it uses the same phrases as the false Charter.

beats.scene: Two riders descend toward a harbour of low white warehouses
beats.summary: Sera and Wick reach Whitehaven, the town where the salt guilds keep their halls.

beats.scene: Maren Tidewell holds up a letter beside a table in a long salt warehouse
beats.summary: Maren Tidewell, head of the salt guilds, shows Sera the royal letter that ordered the fee.

beats.scene: A girl bends over a letter beside a pair of salt scales
beats.summary: The letter carries Lysa's name and the royal seal, but Sera thinks the writing looks strange, though she cannot yet prove it.

beats.scene: A calm woman and a young girl shake hands over a scale of salt
beats.summary: Maren agrees to keep the guilds quiet for three days if Sera can bring proof.

beats.scene: Two armies face each other across a narrow stone bridge over a grey river
beats.summary: Sera and Wick climb a ridge and see the Weigh-Bridge below, with two armies facing each other across it.

beats.scene: An old man in a leather apron sits on a stool beside great scales
beats.summary: The bridge-keeper Tam Greaves refuses to leave his post and tells Sera what the old custom of weighing means.

beats.scene: Soldiers in blue cloaks face a line of loaded iron carts in rain
beats.summary: Tension grows on both banks, and a stone flies from the crowd and clatters on the bridge.

beats.scene: Sera stands alone on the bridge between two armies with a scroll
beats.summary: Sera walks onto the bridge, between both sides, and asks them to wait three days and read the Charter with her.

beats.scene: A woman in armour and a broad man in leather scowl across a bridge
beats.summary: Lysa orders Sera to go home, and Kael says that a girl with a scroll will not stop his iron.

beats.scene: Sera holds up a scroll toward two scowling leaders, her hand steady
beats.summary: Sera says only that the Charter is the law of both lands and that if they truly want war they can read it first.

beats.scene: Lysa, furious, grips the bridge rail while Sera unrolls the old Charter
beats.summary: Kael agrees to wait if Lysa does, and Lysa, furious, steps forward to read the Charter.

beats.scene: A woman in armour goes pale as she reads a parchment
beats.summary: Lysa reads the real clause, goes pale, and says she never ordered a fee.

beats.scene: An old man balances a handful of iron against a handful of salt
beats.summary: Tam Greaves weighs iron against salt, and the two pans balance exactly, which makes the soldiers murmur.

beats.scene: Two groups of soldiers step back a pace from each other
beats.summary: Both armies lower their weapons and step back, and the three days begin.

beats.scene: Lysa looks down at the floor of a tent, ashamed, holding a signed paper
beats.summary: In her tent Lysa admits that on the night of the funeral the Chancellor gave her many papers to sign, and that she signed without reading.

beats.scene: Two sisters sit side by side on a camp bed in a lamplit tent
beats.summary: Sera tells Lysa that nobody blames her for being tired and grieving, and asks what she remembers about the papers.

beats.scene: A tall woman counts on her fingers beside a heap of tent blankets
beats.summary: Lysa remembers orders for supplies and guard postings, and a number of pages she never even turned over.

beats.scene: Lord Kael unfolds a letter and shows it to Sera across a campfire
beats.summary: Kael shows his own letter, which insults him and carries Lysa's seal, and Sera sees it is in the same clerk's handwriting.

beats.scene: A girl points to a small curl on the crossbar of a letter t
beats.summary: Sera shows the others a small curl on the letter t that appears in the false Charter, Kael's letter and Maren's letter.

beats.scene: A hooded scout sits by a fire and draws in the dirt
beats.summary: Brenna Ashmoor, Kael's daughter and a scout, reports that strangers in mixed cloaks have burned an Ash barn without hurting anyone.

beats.scene: Sera draws lines on a map pinned beneath a lantern, Lysa and Kael watching
beats.summary: They ask who gains from a war, and Sera sees that the answer is a Protector who would rule until an heir is found.

beats.scene: Two leaders look at each other across a map, remembering something
beats.summary: Kael and Lysa each remember that Karth once said a kingdom without an heir needs a Protector.

beats.scene: A bridge at night with a fire on each bank and a lantern between
beats.summary: The first night of the truce passes with a fire on each bank and Tam's lantern shining in the middle.

beats.scene: A rider gallops down the hill at night waving a torch
beats.summary: A rider warns that Torren is approaching with a company of Ash lords, many of them armed.

beats.scene: Torren arrives on horseback with Ash lords, then dismounts, ashamed, before his sisters
beats.summary: Torren arrives at the bridge, leaves the Ash lords behind, and walks forward alone, with his head bowed.

beats.scene: A young man kneels on the ground before two women in a tent
beats.summary: Torren confesses that Karth paid his debts to the moneylender Gilder Prowse and told him to keep the Ash lords angry.

beats.scene: Lysa shouts at her brother in a lamplit tent while Sera stands between them
beats.summary: Lysa shouts at Torren, and for a moment it seems the family will break apart.

beats.scene: A broad man in leather watches the quarrel through a gap in the tent
beats.summary: Kael, who has heard everything, says drily that now he knows who was pouring oil on his lords.

beats.scene: Three siblings face each other in the light of a lamp in a tent
beats.summary: Sera calms them and says what matters is proof, and the person who has proof is the clerk who copied the letters.

beats.scene: A smiling young man talks to an angry noble beside a line of horses
beats.summary: Torren uses his charm to talk the hot-headed Lord Garrow Stane out of attacking the bridge.

beats.scene: A girl draws a plan of a palace on the ground with a stick
beats.summary: Sera explains the seal-book at the palace, which records every sealed letter, and how it might prove the Chancellor's lies.

beats.scene: Lysa speaks quietly with Kael by a map while Brenna Ashmoor listens
beats.summary: Lysa and Kael agree a plan: they will keep the truce, and then come to Brinegate when Sera calls a Council.

beats.scene: Four people stand beside saddled horses in cold morning mist
beats.summary: Sera, Torren, Wick and Brenna prepare to ride secretly to Brinegate, with Brenna as Kael's witness.

beats.scene: A tall woman in armour holds her small sister in a tight hug
beats.summary: Lysa embraces Sera and says that she was wrong to think of her as only the little one.

beats.scene: Four riders gallop under a starry sky along a dark river road
beats.summary: Sera, Torren, Wick and Brenna ride through the night toward Brinegate.

beats.scene: Four travellers sit around a tiny fire in a ruined mill
beats.summary: They rest in an old ruined mill, where Brenna teaches Torren how to light a fire and he fails three times.

beats.scene: Four riders lie flat in a ditch as horsemen pass above
beats.summary: A band of riders in mixed cloaks passes along the road, and the four hide in a ditch until they are gone.

beats.scene: A scout creeps through bushes toward two men sitting at a fire
beats.summary: Brenna overhears two of the riders complain that the Chancellor's silver is late.

beats.scene: A king with a kind face shows a small girl a scroll by candlelight
beats.summary: Sera remembers her father teaching her, when she was small, how to read the Charter and why it matters.

beats.scene: A walled city with a river and tall towers at dusk
beats.summary: They reach Brinegate at dusk and find the gates watched by the Chancellor's guards.

beats.scene: Four people crouch behind a fishmonger's cart and roll through a gate
beats.summary: Wick knows a way in: they slip through the river gate hidden among baskets of fish.

beats.scene: A round cook in an apron beckons four visitors into a steamy kitchen
beats.summary: In the palace kitchen the cook Mother Bessel, who once owed Sera a kindness, hides them in the pantry.

beats.scene: Four people walk down a dark stair toward a door with light beneath it
beats.summary: At midnight they creep down the stair to the archive door and knock the old signal.

beats.scene: An old man in a nightcap opens a door beside a hissing cat
beats.summary: Pell opens the door, and Inkwell hisses at Brenna, who has never seen a cat so fierce.

beats.scene: Master Pell opens a heavy book and shows a torn stub of a page
beats.summary: Pell shows the king's seal-book, which records every sealed letter, and a page has been cut out.

beats.scene: A girl runs a finger down a column of dates in a great ledger
beats.summary: Sera reads the entries on either side of the gap and finds letters that are listed but that no longer exist.

beats.scene: A young man peers at a ledger entry and taps it with one finger
beats.summary: Torren spots a payment from the privy purse to Master Prowse, the moneylender, on the same night as his own debts were paid.

beats.scene: Two young scouts creep up a stair behind a tall office door
beats.summary: Brenna and Wick scout the Chancellor's tower and find a narrow stair above his office.

beats.scene: Brenna crouches among quills and scrolls in a small room above a stair
beats.summary: Above the Chancellor's office they find Fennick's workroom, covered with practice sheets of Lysa's signature.

beats.scene: A girl sorts through papers on a slanted desk by a candle
beats.summary: Among the sheets Sera finds the changed clause of the Charter written again and again, and copies of Kael's seal.

beats.scene: Footsteps run down the stair as three people hide behind a screen
beats.summary: They hear a door slam and a clerk's frightened footsteps running away down the stair.

beats.scene: A smiling man in velvet blocks a dim corridor
beats.summary: The Chancellor appears in the corridor and politely tells Sera she is tired and should rest.

beats.scene: Sera stands tall facing the Chancellor with her siblings beside her
beats.summary: Sera announces that, by the old law, the Council will meet in two days, at dawn, in the Hall of Two Crowns, and Karth smiles and agrees.

beats.scene: A key turns in a lock as four people stare at an archive door
beats.summary: Back in the archive they hear a heavy key turn in the lock outside, and they are shut in.

beats.scene: Four people stand in a dim archive staring at the locked door
beats.summary: Locked in, Torren pounds on the door and Pell sighs, while Karth's guards stand silent outside.

beats.scene: Sera spreads an old palace plan across a table beneath a lamp
beats.summary: Sera remembers an old plan of the palace and finds a stair marked behind the archive's last shelf.

beats.scene: Sera and Pell climb a narrow secret stair behind a bookshelf
beats.summary: Pell pulls a certain book, a shelf swings open, and the group climbs a narrow stair no one has used in years.

beats.scene: An old man ties small letters to white doves on a dark rooftop
beats.summary: On a rooftop Pell sends his doves to Lysa, Kael and Maren with the same message: come to the Hall of Two Crowns at dawn.

beats.scene: Four friends whisper in a dark tunnel, then hurry in different directions
beats.summary: They split: Torren will find the moneylender Prowse, while Wick and Brenna will find the missing clerk.

beats.scene: A young courier and a scout ask questions in a smoky tavern
beats.summary: Wick and Brenna search the lower town, asking at taverns and laundries for a clerk with inky fingers.

beats.scene: A trembling clerk hides in a shed full of candles and barrels
beats.summary: They find Hob Fennick hiding in a chandler's shed, afraid and ink-stained.

beats.scene: A thin clerk in a shed speaks quickly to a courier and a scout
beats.summary: Fennick says the Chancellor threatened him and that he wants to confess, but only if he is not punished.

beats.scene: Two people lead a hooded man through a crowd of market porters
beats.summary: Wick promises Sera will ask the Council for mercy, and they smuggle Fennick toward the palace in a porter's coat.

beats.scene: Torren sits across a table from a nervous moneylender with a thick ledger
beats.summary: Torren visits Prowse's counting house, and his honest charm persuades the moneylender to bring his ledger to the hall.

beats.scene: Sera sits wide awake in a dark stair, rehearsing words under her breath
beats.summary: Sera cannot sleep, and Pell tells her that an argument is only a bridge made of true planks.

beats.scene: A white dove perches at a window with a tiny scroll on its leg
beats.summary: Before dawn three doves return, with replies from Lysa, Kael and Maren: they are coming.

beats.scene: Pale light creeps across a great hall as servants light torches
beats.summary: Dawn comes, and servants open the great doors of the Hall of Two Crowns.

beats.scene: Four figures slip through a servants' door carrying a hooded clerk and a ledger
beats.summary: Wick, Brenna, Torren, Prowse and Fennick slip into the hall by the servants' door.

beats.scene: Lysa in armour and Kael in leather stride side by side into a hall
beats.summary: Lysa and Kael ride into the city with their guards and enter the hall side by side.

beats.scene: Maren Tidewell leads a line of guild masters in white into a hall
beats.summary: Maren arrives with the salt guild masters, and the hall begins to fill with people of both lands.

beats.scene: A great hall fills with lords, merchants and guards under two crowns
beats.summary: The Hall of Two Crowns fills with the Salt Guard, the Ash lords and the salt guilds.

beats.scene: The Chancellor enters last, smiling, and takes a place near the crowns
beats.summary: Chancellor Karth enters last, confident and smiling, and takes his place beside the crowns.

beats.scene: The Chancellor addresses the silent hall with one hand lifted
beats.summary: Karth speaks first, blaming the Ash lords and offering to rule as Protector to restore order.

beats.scene: A murmuring crowd of lords, some nodding, some frowning
beats.summary: Some lords nod, tired of fear, and Sera feels the mood of the hall begin to tilt toward the Chancellor.

beats.scene: Sera steps forward with the old Charter and a pile of practice sheets
beats.summary: Sera steps forward with the Charter, the practice sheets and the seal-book, and calls Hob Fennick.

beats.scene: A trembling clerk walks toward the middle of a silent hall
beats.summary: Fennick shuffles forward, shaking, while the Chancellor glares at him across the hall.

beats.scene: A trembling clerk speaks while the Chancellor glares across the hall
beats.summary: Fennick confesses that he copied the Halvane signatures and changed the Charter's clause on the Chancellor's orders.

beats.scene: The Chancellor raises one hand and speaks sharply in the hall
beats.summary: Karth says that this is only the word of a frightened clerk, and Sera replies, then let him write.

beats.scene: A clerk writes at a small table while the whole hall watches
beats.summary: Fennick writes Lysa's signature in front of everyone, and it matches the letters exactly.

beats.scene: Sera lays practice sheets beside the false letters under a window
beats.summary: Sera lays the practice sheets beside the letters, and the same small curl appears on every t.

beats.scene: Pell holds the true and the false Charter side by side before the lords
beats.summary: Pell reads both clauses aloud, and the hall hears the difference between weight for weight and a fee.

beats.scene: A thick ledger is placed on a table before the silent lords
beats.summary: Prowse lays his ledger on the table and shows payments from the privy purse, which Torren's debts were paid from.

beats.scene: Torren steps out of the crowd, pale, and addresses the hall
beats.summary: Torren stands and confesses that Karth paid his debts, proving the Chancellor's plan, at the cost of his own pride.

beats.scene: Lysa and Kael stand in front of the hall, holding their false letters
beats.summary: Lysa and Kael each admit they were fooled, and the hall realises both sides were tricked.

beats.scene: Guards lead the Chancellor away from the hall as the crowd watches in silence
beats.summary: The hall demands Karth's removal, and he is taken away, to be judged by a court of both lands.

beats.scene: The great doors close on a hall left silent beneath two crowns
beats.summary: The doors close behind him, and the hall is silent, for a long moment.

beats.scene: The crowns glimmer as the crowd turns to look at Sera
beats.summary: With the Chancellor gone, the question of the crown returns, and Lysa and Torren say Sera deserves it.

beats.scene: A young woman looks up at two crowns, her hands behind her back
beats.summary: Sera hesitates, because she is only seventeen and she knows how heavy a crown can be.

beats.scene: Lord Kael and Maren Tidewell stand with arms folded in front of the crowns
beats.summary: Kael and Maren say they want a share of power, so that no single Halvane can rule them again.

beats.scene: Lords of both lands shout across a hall while Pell waves his arms
beats.summary: The hall breaks into argument about who should hold power, and for a moment the peace seems fragile.

beats.scene: Sera opens the Charter's last page in front of the crowds
beats.summary: Sera finds the Charter's old promise that disputes should be weighed at a table of equal seats.

beats.scene: Sera holds up the old Charter and points to a clause
beats.summary: Sera proposes a Council of Salt and Ash, with three seats for each land, a Halvane at its head without a vote, and the Archivist to keep the record.

beats.scene: Hands rise one by one in a hall, Ash and salt side by side
beats.summary: Kael asks who breaks a tie, and Maren answers dryly that a level scale means nobody has yet given the other side a reason, and the first hands go up.

beats.scene: Three siblings sit on a palace rooftop above a city of lights
beats.summary: That night the three Halvanes sit on the roof, and Torren asks whether they still get the crown, and Sera reminds him that the clock is still running.

beats.scene: Workers cast a great set of scales from molten iron and white salt-glass
beats.summary: The Scales of Two Crowns are cast at the Weigh-Bridge from iron and salt-glass.

beats.scene: Iron smiths and salt glassmakers argue over a drawing beside a roaring forge
beats.summary: Smiths from Cindermoor and glassmakers from Saltmarch quarrel over the shape of the scales, then agree.

beats.scene: A huge pair of scales is raised on a stone arch above a bridge
beats.summary: The scales are hung above the Weigh-Bridge, and the crowd cheers as Tam Greaves tests them.

beats.scene: Carts loaded with iron and salt roll past each other across a bridge
beats.summary: The first iron carts cross the bridge and salt carts come back the other way, weight for weight.

beats.scene: A scribe copies a long scroll while an old man watches
beats.summary: Sera has the true Charter copied by hand, with Fennick doing the copying, and posts it in every market.

beats.scene: A girl and a courier ride past a glowing furnace in dark hills
beats.summary: Sera and Wick visit Cindermoor, where Kael shows her the ironworks and the Deepwell mine.

beats.scene: Maren shows Sera a gleaming salt pan at sunrise
beats.summary: In Saltmarch Maren shows Sera the pans again, and Edda tells her that salt is already cheaper.

beats.scene: Sera rides through green fields and white salt pans, talking with farmers
beats.summary: Over the following months Sera travels between both lands, and the trade begins to heal them.

beats.scene: Lords and guild masters argue at a long table, Pell writing quickly
beats.summary: The first Council meeting is long and noisy, with Garrow Stane complaining, and Pell records every word.

beats.scene: A young man in plain clothes sits at a desk full of ledgers
beats.summary: Torren sells his fine horses, repays Prowse and learns to keep the Council's honest accounts.

beats.scene: Snow falls over white salt pans and a row of grey huts
beats.summary: Winter comes, and snow falls over the white salt pans.

beats.scene: Maren stands on a cracked sea wall pointing at dark clouds
beats.summary: Maren warns that a great storm is coming and that the old sea wall is cracked.

beats.scene: Lords around a table argue and point in different directions
beats.summary: The Council argues about who should pay for the sea wall, and Garrow Stane says it is not Ash business.

beats.scene: Rain lashes salt pans as miners drive iron stakes into a sea wall
beats.summary: Kael sends Ash miners with iron stakes and tools to help build the sea wall.

beats.scene: A long line of miners in sleet walks down a coast road with tools
beats.summary: Brenna leads a column of miners down the coast road through sleet.

beats.scene: Salt Guard soldiers and Ash miners carry stones together at night
beats.summary: Lysa has the Salt Guard carry stones, and soldiers and miners work side by side all night.

beats.scene: Torren ladles soup from a huge pot to hundreds of tired workers
beats.summary: Torren organises bread and hot soup for the workers, using his charm to beg every baker on the coast.

beats.scene: Huge waves crash against a wall while people hold lanterns
beats.summary: The storm hits at midnight, and the waves crash against the sea wall.

beats.scene: A girl carries a child through knee-deep water beside a hut
beats.summary: Sera helps Edda's family out of a flooding hut and carries the village records to the high ground.

beats.scene: Exhausted workers sleep side by side on sacks of salt at dawn
beats.summary: The wall holds, and at dawn miners and guards sleep together on the salt sacks until Garrow Stane arrives with timber.

beats.scene: Frost on green shoots in a grey hillside field
beats.summary: A late spring frost ruins the Ash Hills harvest.

beats.scene: A girl talks quietly with a scout on a hillside above a mine
beats.summary: Brenna tells Sera that families in Cindermoor are hungry, though her proud father will not ask for help.

beats.scene: Sera speaks to the Council with a hand on the Charter
beats.summary: Sera brings it to the Council, and Maren says the salt guilds have fish and salt to spare.

beats.scene: Wagons loaded with barrels of salt fish roll toward grey hills in spring
beats.summary: Wagons loaded with barrels of salted fish roll toward the hills.

beats.scene: A salt-raker girl and a scout walk beside a wagon
beats.summary: Edda travels with the wagons and finds that Brenna is better company than she expected.

beats.scene: Hill families unload barrels in a stone village while children cheer
beats.summary: Hill families receive the barrels, and a miner's wife shares the first pickled fish with the drivers.

beats.scene: Kael hands an iron plough to Maren in a cold square
beats.summary: Kael thanks Maren awkwardly and sends back a gift of iron ploughshares, weight for weight.

beats.scene: Torn notices flutter on a wall at night in Brinegate
beats.summary: New notices appear at night, claiming the Council is weak and that the Halvanes want to rule alone.

beats.scene: Crowds queue at an open archive door while a baker reads a large book
beats.summary: Sera opens the archive to the public so that anyone can read every Council order in the Open Book, and a baker finds that the bread tax was never raised.

beats.scene: A thin clerk points at a torn notice before the Council
beats.summary: Hob recognises the hand of the notices as Dunstan Pike's, a bitter copyist, and the Council sets him to copy the Open Book as his penance.

beats.scene: A tall ship with bright sails glides into Pan Harbour
beats.summary: A ship from the rich land of Varenna sails into Pan Harbour.

beats.scene: An envoy in a feathered hat bows before three siblings
beats.summary: A foreign envoy, Casimir Dorne, offers friendship and asks to speak with each land separately.

beats.scene: A smooth envoy pours wine for a smiling young man at a banquet
beats.summary: The envoy dines with Torren and flatters him, hoping to buy iron cheaply and divide the kingdom.

beats.scene: Torren grins at a table while the envoy leans in
beats.summary: Torren recognises the same tune that Karth once played and pretends to listen, to learn more.

beats.scene: A tall woman in armour pushes a chest of swords back across a table
beats.summary: The envoy sends a hundred fine swords as a gift to the Salt Guard, and Lysa sends them back politely.

beats.scene: A broad man stands with a bag of gold at his feet and scowls
beats.summary: An agent of the envoy brings Kael a secret offer of gold for his iron, while Brenna listens behind a curtain.

beats.scene: Kael lays the envoy's offer on the Council table before all the seats
beats.summary: Kael brings the offer to the Council in the open.

beats.scene: An envoy stands before a Council of both lands, looking uneasy
beats.summary: The envoy speaks before the whole Council and finds that he cannot divide them.

beats.scene: Maren leans over a table and slides a document across it
beats.summary: Maren proposes a fair treaty with Varenna that trades with both lands on the Charter's weights.

beats.scene: A tall ship sails out of a harbour at sunset
beats.summary: The ship sails away with the treaty, and Sera notes that the Charter is stronger because it was tested.

beats.scene: Lysa listens carefully to a miner who gestures, while Sera watches and smiles
beats.summary: Lysa learns to listen to the people she once only commanded, and the Council grows stronger.

beats.scene: Soldiers learn mining knots while miners learn to tie sailors' knots
beats.summary: The Salt Guard and the Ash miners swap skills: sea knots and rescue ropes in return for mine tunnels and tools.

beats.scene: A judge in grey robes sits before a court of twelve at the Weigh-Bridge
beats.summary: The Court of Both Lands meets at the Weigh-Bridge, with Judge Tamsin Rook presiding, to hear the case against Karth.

beats.scene: A thin man in grey stands before a court with chained hands
beats.summary: Karth, thin and calm, refuses to repent, and says he only wanted order.

beats.scene: A girl in a plain dress gives evidence with books in her arms
beats.summary: Sera gives evidence from the archive, and the seal-book and the practice sheets speak for themselves.

beats.scene: A judge reads a verdict as the court waits in silence
beats.summary: The Court strips Karth of every office and sends him away from Haldmere forever.

beats.scene: A thin man looks back at a girl from a departing wagon
beats.summary: Karth tells Sera that she will find the crown heavier than she thinks, and she answers that she does not mean to wear one.

beats.scene: A girl and an old man walk beside the river at dusk
beats.summary: Sera feels hollow after the trial, and Pell says that nobody cheers a ledger but that truth is still the best foundation.

beats.scene: A courier and a scout race horses along a long straight road
beats.summary: Wick becomes Chief Courier of the Council, and he and Brenna carry letters that carry both seals.

beats.scene: A smuggler holds up a false weight while an old man tests it
beats.summary: A smuggler tries to cross the Weigh-Bridge with false weights, and Tam Greaves catches him with the Scales of Two Crowns.

beats.scene: Children weigh feathers against pebbles at a harvest fair
beats.summary: At summer's end the first Weigh-Day festival fills the Weigh-Bridge with music and dancing.

beats.scene: Three siblings stand awake at night before the two crowns
beats.summary: On the night before the year and a day ends, the three Halvanes meet in the hall and wonder.

beats.scene: Master Pell stands in the Hall of Two Crowns holding a sealed envelope
beats.summary: A year and a day have passed, and Pell opens a sealed envelope that the old king gave him.

beats.scene: Lords of both lands rise one after another to speak
beats.summary: Pell reads the last clause: the people of salt and ash will name the keeper of the peace, and Kael, Maren and the others each name Sera.

beats.scene: Sera opens a small wooden box and finds a folded letter beside the crowns
beats.summary: Sera finds a small box beside the crowns, and in it a folded letter from her father.

beats.scene: A girl reads a letter in her father's handwriting with tears in her eyes
beats.summary: Her father writes that he suspected the Chancellor but lacked proof, and that the will was a test of who would read before signing.

beats.scene: A hand holds a letter with one line underlined
beats.summary: He writes that a crown that is given is only a hat, but one that is earned is a bridge.

beats.scene: Sera stands before the Council with both crowns on a table beside her
beats.summary: Sera accepts the rule, but sets both crowns upon the Council table and keeps a simple ring of iron and salt-glass.

beats.scene: A hall of cheering lords and soldiers beating drums
beats.summary: The hall cheers, soldiers and miners beat time together, and Pell wipes his eyes.

beats.scene: Sera writes at a desk by lamplight while her siblings watch from the doorway
beats.summary: That evening Sera writes the first page of a new chronicle, and her siblings join her in the archive.

A1A2: King Edric dies in the night, and his three children cry.
The bells ring, and all of Brinegate wakes to hear the sad news.
Two old crowns rest in a great hall, one white and one black.
The three children eat a cold supper, and nobody wants to speak.
A long line of sad people follows the king's coffin to the river.
At the supper Sera finds the Chancellor taking papers from her father's desk.
He smiles, and says the king's papers must be kept safe.

Lysa leaves for the border, and Torren rides away laughing.

Old Master Pell gives her tea, and his grey cat watches.
Sera shows Pell the will, and he reads it twice.
Pell teaches her how to tell one writer from another.
Pell gives Sera an iron key to the deepest room.

She reads how the first Halvane king ended the old wars.

Sera reads the notice and stops at one line.

Pell looks at both papers and says someone changed it on purpose.
Pell warns her that blaming the Chancellor is very dangerous.
Pell tells her about a clerk who spoke without proof.
Sera starts a secret notebook of every changed word.
She hides the true Charter among boring old tax books.
Sera walks through the palace and acts as if nothing is wrong.
A tired rider brings news from the border bridge.
At the bridge, soldiers stop every cart that carries iron.
Torren pays for big feasts and makes many promises.
Lord Kael reads a letter that insults him, and he is angry.
Torren brings Sera the angry reply from Lord Kael.
Sera says Lysa would never write such an insult.
At supper, Torren says the Ash lords would make him king.
Sera sees a light in the Chancellor's tower every night.
Sera and Pell agree that someone must go to the bridge.
At dawn, Sera and Wick leave the palace on two horses.
Sera and Wick ride east along the white salt road.
Sera sees the salt pans, flat and bright like a lake.
A young salt worker says everything costs twice as much now.
The market is quiet, and people blame the Ash lords.
An old woman says the Ash lords will attack soon.
A man reads a loud notice about the Ash lords.
They ride into Whitehaven, the town of the salt guilds.
Maren Tidewell shows Sera the royal letter about the fee.
Sera looks at the letter and thinks the writing looks odd.
Maren agrees to wait three days for Sera's proof.
From a hill, they see two armies facing each other.
An old man sits on the bridge and will not move.
A stone flies from the crowd and hits the bridge.
Sera walks onto the bridge between the two armies.
Lysa tells Sera to go home, and Kael laughs.
Sera says the Charter is the law of both lands.
Kael agrees to wait if Lysa waits too.
Lysa reads the true clause and her face turns pale.
Tam weighs iron against salt, and the scales balance.
Both armies step back, and the three days begin.
Lysa says she signed many papers without reading them.
Sera says nobody blames her for being tired and sad.
Lysa remembers orders for supplies and guard posts.
Kael shows Sera his own letter, and it looks strange.
Sera points to a little curl on the letter t.
Brenna, Kael's daughter, says strangers burned a barn.
Sera draws a map and asks who gains from a war.
Kael and Lysa both remember the word Protector.
The first night is quiet, with a fire on each bank.
A rider warns that Torren is coming with many lords.
Torren stops his horse and walks to the bridge alone.
Torren says the Chancellor paid his debts for him.
Lysa shouts at her brother, and Sera stands between them.
Kael says that now he knows who made his lords so angry.
Sera says they need proof, not more shouting.
Torren talks to an angry lord and calms him.
Sera tells them about the seal-book in the palace.
Lysa and Kael agree to keep the peace and come to Brinegate.
Sera, Torren, Wick and Brenna get ready to ride.
Lysa hugs her little sister and says she was wrong.
The four riders race through the dark toward Brinegate.
They rest in an old mill, and Torren cannot light a fire.
They hide in a ditch as strange riders pass by.
Brenna hears two men say the Chancellor's silver is late.
Sera remembers her father teaching her to read the Charter.
They see Brinegate at dusk, with guards at every gate.
They hide behind fish baskets and roll into the city.
Mother Bessel the cook hides them in her pantry.
At midnight, they go down to the archive and knock.
Pell opens the door, and his cat is very angry.
Pell shows them the seal-book, and a page is cut out.
Sera reads the numbers and finds letters that are missing.
Torren sees a payment to Prowse in the book.
Brenna and Wick look for a way into the Chancellor's tower.
Above the office they find a small room full of papers.
Sera finds the false clause written again and again.
A thin clerk sees them and runs away down the stair.
The Chancellor stands in the corridor and smiles at Sera.
Sera says there will be a Council in two days.
Back in the archive, they hear a key turn outside.
Torren hits the locked door, and Pell sighs.
Sera remembers an old map of the palace.
Pell pulls a book, and a shelf opens like a door.
On the roof, Pell sends white doves with messages.
They split up, and each goes a different way.
Wick and Brenna ask about a clerk with black fingers.
They find the clerk hiding in a shed full of candles.
Hob says the Chancellor scared him, and he wants to help.
Wick promises mercy, and they dress Hob as a porter.
Torren talks to Prowse and asks him for his big book.
Sera cannot sleep, and Pell gives her wise words.
Three doves return with notes from Lysa, Kael and Maren.
Dawn comes, and servants open the doors of the Hall.
Wick, Brenna, Torren and Hob slip in by a small door.
Lysa and Kael walk into the hall side by side.
Maren leads the salt guild masters into the hall.
The hall fills with soldiers, lords and merchants.
The Chancellor comes in last, smiling, and takes his place.
Karth speaks first and says the Ash lords are to blame.
Some lords nod, and the crowd begins to agree with him.
Sera steps forward with the Charter and calls Hob Fennick.
A shaking clerk walks slowly into the middle of the hall.
Hob says he copied the signatures for the Chancellor.
Karth says a frightened clerk cannot be trusted.
Hob writes Lysa's name, and the hall watches him.
Sera shows the same small curl on every letter t.
Pell reads out the true clause and then the false one.
Prowse puts his big book on the table for everyone.
Torren stands up and says the Chancellor paid his debts.
Lysa and Kael say they were both fooled too.
The hall shouts, and the guards take the Chancellor away.
The doors close, and the hall is silent for a long time.
Now everyone looks at Sera, and at the crowns.
Sera looks at the crowns and does not want them.
Kael and Maren say they want a share of the power.
The lords argue loudly about who should rule.
Sera reads the last page of the old Charter.
Sera suggests a Council with three seats for each land.
Hands go up one by one, Ash and salt side by side.
That night the three Halvanes sit together on the roof.
Workers pour hot iron and white glass into a huge mould.
Iron workers and glass workers argue about the scales.
The great scales hang above the bridge, and people cheer.
Iron carts and salt carts cross the bridge, weight for weight.
Hob copies the true Charter, and it is put up everywhere.
Sera and Wick ride to Cindermoor and see the iron mines.
Maren shows Sera the salt pans, and Edda smiles.
Sera rides through both lands and talks with many people.

Torren sells his horses and learns to keep honest accounts.

The visitor bows to the three Halvanes and smiles a lot.

B1B2: Old King Edric Halvane dies in his bed at midnight, and the bells of Brinegate begin to ring. His three children stand beside him, and none of them knows what will happen next.

All through the night the great bells ring over Brinegate, and people come out of their houses in their nightclothes. Nobody needs to be told what the sound means, because the old king has been ill for a long time.
In the Hall of Two Crowns, the pale Salt Crown and the dark Ash Crown rest side by side. Long ago, they joined the salty coast and the iron hills into one kingdom.
Lysa, Torren and Sera sit at the long table and push their food around their plates. Each of them is thinking about the crown, but nobody wants to be the first to say it.
On the day of the funeral, the whole city walks behind the coffin toward the river. Salt lords walk on one side and Ash lords walk on the other, and they do not speak to each other.
During the funeral supper, Sera slips away to her father's study to be alone for a moment. Instead she finds Chancellor Karth in his velvet coat, quietly gathering papers from the king's desk.

Karth smiles and says that a kingdom cannot stop for grief, and that someone must keep its business safe. Then he carries a thick bundle of papers away toward Lysa's rooms, and Sera thinks no more about it.
The next morning, the lords crowd into the great hall, and Karth unrolls the king's will. It names no heir, but it says the crown will go to whoever keeps salt and ash at peace for a year and a day.

Lysa says that peace is kept by soldiers, and she orders the Salt Guard to march to the border at once. Torren laughs, calls for his horse, and rides off to win friends in the Ash Hills with feasts and flattery.
That night Sera sits alone in her father's study, looking at the empty desk. She decides that if the will is a test, then someone should find out what was really agreed between the two lands.
The next morning Sera goes down the long spiral stair to the archive beneath the palace. She has been an apprentice there for two years, and the smell of old paper always makes her feel calm.
Master Pell, the old Archivist, is already at his desk with tea and his grey cat, Inkwell. He does not mention the king, but he tells her that grief is best faced with work.
Sera shows Pell how strangely the will is worded, with its odd phrase about a year and a day. Pell reads it twice and says that someone ought to read what was actually agreed.
Pell holds a glass over two samples of handwriting and shows her how every writer leaves habits behind. The shape of a loop, the slant of a line and the pressure of a pen can all give a person away.
Pell takes a small iron key from a hook and puts it in her hand. It opens the deep vault, where the oldest treaties of Haldmere are kept.
Sera carries a lamp down the cold stone stair and unlocks the heavy door at the bottom. Beyond it, shelves of dusty parchment stretch away into the dark.
After an hour of searching, Sera finds the original Salt Charter, written on dry yellow parchment in neat old script. It says in plain words that iron and salt are to be traded weight for weight.
As Sera reads on, she learns how the first Halvane king ended the old wars between the coast and the hills. The Charter promises great scales at the bridge, and no fee to be asked by either side.
A young royal courier with a muddy satchel bursts into the archive, out of breath and grinning. He is Wick, and his joke about Pell's cat makes Sera laugh for the first time in days.
Later Wick whispers to Sera that the Chancellor has ordered every royal letter to be handed to him alone. Couriers used to carry them straight to their owners, and he does not like the change.
A herald in a blue coat nails a fresh copy of the Salt Charter to a post in the market square. Soon a crowd gathers to read it, because everyone has heard rumours about the border.
Sera pushes to the front of the crowd and reads the posted Charter slowly. Then she stops, because one clause does not say what she read in the vault.

That evening, in the vault, Sera lays her careful copy of the notice beside the old Charter. The true clause says weight for weight with no fee, but the posted one says that iron must now pay a fee to the crown.

The false clause calls the fee a levy, a word that no scribe of the old days ever used. Somebody who writes in the modern way has changed the Charter, and has not been careful enough to copy the old voice.
Pell studies the two copies for a long time, turning them under the lamp. At last he agrees that nobody could make such a change by accident.
Pell warns Sera that accusing the Chancellor without proof would be dangerous. Karth holds the royal seal, and the Palace Watch answers to him.
Pell tells her about a clerk who once accused a lord without proof. The clerk was sent away to a far post, and nobody ever heard from him again.
Sera decides to gather proof quietly, and she begins a secret notebook. In it she writes every difference between the true Charter and the false one.
Sera hides the true Charter between dull tax ledgers on a high shelf, where no thief would ever look. Pell says the best place to hide a thing is among things that nobody reads.
Sera walks through the palace with a stack of books, past two guards in grey, as if she were still only a sad apprentice. She smiles at everyone, and she thinks very hard.
A tired rider arrives at the archive door, covered in mud, with news from the border. He says the Salt Guard has begun stopping iron carts at the Weigh-Bridge.
At the Weigh-Bridge the soldiers demand the new fee from every driver. Many of the drivers cannot pay, so they turn back with their heavy loads of iron.
In Cindermoor, Torren spends gold on feasts for the Ash lords and promises everything to everyone. The lords like him, and they like his wine even more.
Lord Kael Ashmoor, the master of the Ash Hills ironworks, receives a letter with Lysa's seal that insults him and his people. He writes back that he will close the mines unless the carts are freed.
Torren hurries back to Brinegate and shows Sera Kael's furious reply, which he was given to carry. It says that unless the iron carts are freed, the Ash mines will close.
Sera says that Lysa would never write such an insult, even in her worst temper. Torren only shrugs and says that Lysa is proud and has surprised them before.
At a palace supper Torren, flushed with wine, boasts that the Ash lords would gladly crown him. He laughs and says they might even divide the kingdom between them.
Sera notices that the Chancellor's window burns every night, long after the rest of the palace is dark. Couriers come and go beneath it, carrying sealed letters in the dark.
Sera and Pell lean over a map and agree that someone must reach the bridge before the soldiers start fighting. Pell is too old to ride, so the task is clearly Sera's.

Sera takes the true Charter from its hiding place and packs her notebook, and at dawn Wick waits at the gate with two horses. Nobody tries to stop them, and she does not know whether that is good or bad.
Sera and Wick leave Brinegate behind and ride east along the old white salt road. The wheels of ten thousand carts have worn it smooth, and the air begins to smell of the sea.
Riding through Saltmarch, Sera sees the vast salt pans for the first time, flat and shining like a frozen lake. Workers with long wooden rakes drag the white crystals into low mounds.
A young salt-raker called Edda leans on her rake and tells Sera that prices have doubled since the iron stopped. Families in her village cannot afford bread, and some are going hungry.

Footsteps pounded down the stair, and a young royal courier burst into the archive with a mud-spattered satchel swinging from his shoulder and a grin that seemed too wide for the room. His name was Wick, he told them breathlessly, and he had been riding since dawn with a message for the Archivist, which he had nearly forgotten in his hurry to see whether the famous cat really bit. Sera, who had not laughed once since the king died, was surprised to find herself laughing now.

Before he left, Wick drew Sera aside beside a tall shelf and lowered his voice, glancing at the stair as though the walls might carry tales. The Chancellor had ordered that every royal letter must pass through his own hands before travelling any farther, and no courier was to deliver a message that had not first been read in the tower. He did not understand why a man who valued peace would wish to open everyone's mail.

Three days after the reading of the will, a herald in a blue coat marched into Brinegate's market square and nailed a freshly written copy of the Salt Charter to the tall wooden post where public notices were always hung. A crowd gathered at once, drawn by the rumours of trouble at the border, and those who could read began to murmur the words aloud for those who could not. It was, the herald announced, the Chancellor's wish that every citizen should know the law of the two lands.

Sera pushed her way to the front of the crowd, as she had done a hundred times at a hundred notices, and read the posted Charter slowly from top to bottom. Halfway down the page her eyes stopped as if they had struck a wall, because the clause about the bridge did not say what she had read in the cold silence of the vault only days before. She read it again, and then a third time, and the words stayed stubbornly different.

That evening, in the vault, Sera laid her careful copy of the notice beside the original Charter and compared them line by line, her lamp wavering above the two pages. The old clause promised weight for weight with no fee on either side, while the posted version had been altered so that every iron cart must pay a fee to the crown before it crossed the bridge. It was a change of only a dozen words, exactly the kind of change a tired reader would never notice, and exactly the kind that could start a war.

Looking closer, Sera noticed that the false clause used the word levy, a stiff modern term that appeared nowhere else in the Charter or in any treaty of the old scribes, who had always written plain words like toll. It was the kind of slip that only a person who spent her days among old documents would catch. Somebody who wrote in the fashion of the present day had altered the Charter, and had not been careful enough to copy the old voice.

Pell studied the two copies for a very long time, turning them under the lamp and humming a low, tuneless note that Sera knew meant he was thinking hard. At last he put down his lens and agreed that no honest slip of the pen could have exchanged a promise of fair weights for a fee on one land's goods. Inkwell, sensing the mood, climbed down from the shelf and sat solemnly on the false notice, as if to hold it in place.

Pell lowered his voice, though nobody but the cat could hear, and warned her that an accusation without proof would be worse than silence. Chancellor Karth held the royal seal, controlled the Palace Watch, and spoke so smoothly that people would believe him against a girl of seventeen even if the girl were telling the truth. If she spoke too soon, he said, she would give the man time to hide what he had done and every reason to silence her.

Pell sat for a while in silence, one hand resting on the cat, before he told her about a clerk he had trained long ago. The young man had accused a powerful lord of stealing from the treasury, but he had shown no proof, and within a month he was posted to a lonely outpost on the northern marshes, where nobody heard from him again. Pell did not say what the clerk's name had been, and Sera understood that it was a name he still found hard to speak.

Sera made up her mind to do what Pell would have done in her place, which was to collect the evidence quietly until it could not be denied. She opened a small notebook with a plain brown cover and began to list, in her smallest handwriting, every difference between the true Charter and the false, along with the date and place she had discovered it. It was a modest beginning, but she knew that great doors are sometimes opened by very small keys.

To keep the original safe, Sera rolled it carefully in clean linen and slid it between two enormous ledgers of forgotten tax receipts on the highest shelf of the archive. Pell watched her from his chair with the first real smile she had seen on his face since the king died, and observed that the finest hiding place in the world was among the things nobody ever wanted to read. Inkwell, who held no opinion whatever about taxes, settled himself comfortably on top of them and went to sleep.

Over the next two days Sera walked through the palace corridors with a stack of books in her arms, nodding politely to the guards in grey cloaks and pretending to be nothing more than a grieving apprentice on an errand. Every smile she gave felt like a small lie, and every footstep behind her felt like a question, but nobody stopped her, and nobody seemed to guess what she carried in her notebook. She had learned, at seventeen, that being overlooked can be a kind of protection.

The next morning a rider stumbled down the archive stair, grey with road dust and swaying from exhaustion, and delivered his news in breathless fragments. The Salt Guard, he said, had closed the Weigh-Bridge to every cart of iron, and the drivers were being turned back unless they could pay a new fee that nobody had heard of a week before. Sera felt the cold of the vault creep up her spine, for the false clause had begun to do exactly what it was written to do.

At the Weigh-Bridge, rows of soldiers in blue cloaks now stood in front of the great gate, demanding the new fee from every driver who tried to cross with iron. The drivers, who had hauled their carts along the same road for thirty years without paying a coin, argued, shouted and finally turned back, leaving the road clogged with angry men and idle oxen. On the far side of the river the salt carts waited too, for no honest trade can flow in only one direction.

Meanwhile in Cindermoor, Torren was making himself the most popular guest in the Ash Hills, filling the long tables of the lords with roast meat and wine he could not afford and promising anything to anyone who raised a cup. He was a gifted talker, quick with a joke and a toast, and the lords, who had always thought of the Halvanes as stiff and distant, found him a pleasant surprise. What none of them noticed was that he never said what he would actually do.

In his smoky ironworks at Ironhold, Lord Kael Ashmoor read a letter bearing the royal seal and Lysa's signature, and the muscles in his broad jaw tightened with every line. It called the Ash lords greedy and ungrateful, accused them of hoarding iron, and warned that the Salt Guard would treat any cart crossing the bridge without a fee as a thief's cart. Kael crumpled the paper in his fist, wrote two lines in reply, and swore that the mines would close and the furnaces go cold before he paid a coin.

Torren rode back to Brinegate in two days, dusty and uncharacteristically serious, and showed Sera the letter that Kael had pressed into his hand for Lysa. By the light of a single candle she read the blunt, angry lines promising that the Ash mines would be shut and the Salt Coast would soon learn what life was like without iron. It was the first time she had ever seen her brother frightened, and he hid it badly.

Sera read the Ash lord's complaint again and said slowly that it simply did not sound like Lysa, who was stubborn and fierce but who had never in her life been petty or cruel in writing. Torren shrugged with the easy carelessness of a man who prefers not to examine things too closely, and replied that pride makes fools of the best of people. Sera did not argue, but she wrote the word insult in her notebook and underlined it twice.

At the next palace supper, Torren, bright-eyed with wine and flattery, leaned back in his chair and announced to the whole table that the Ash lords would gladly crown him if he asked. He laughed, and added, as a joke that was not entirely a joke, that they might divide the kingdom between them and be done with the quarrel. A hush fell over the room, and at the far end of the table the Chancellor lifted his goblet in a smile that never reached his eyes.

Night after night, from the window of the archive stair, Sera watched the single lit window in the Chancellor's tower, glowing long after the rest of the palace had gone dark. Couriers crossed the courtyard beneath it at all hours, small hurried figures carrying sealed packets that vanished into the tower and came out again lighter or heavier. She did not yet know what a man could write at that hour, but she was beginning to suspect that it was not condolences.

By candlelight, Sera and Pell bent over a map and traced the road from Brinegate to the Weigh-Bridge, measuring the days a letter would take to get there and the hours needed to stop a battle. The Chancellor's couriers could not be trusted with any message, Pell said, and his own old bones had not sat a horse in twenty years. It was a short conversation, because both of them had known the answer before they began.

In the grey hour before dawn, Sera took the true Charter, packed it into her saddlebags with her notebook and a loaf of bread, and slipped out to the gate where Wick held two horses. She did not look up at the Chancellor's tower, but she felt the weight of someone's gaze on her back as they clattered under the arch. Nobody stopped them, and Sera could not decide whether that was a mercy or a warning.

Sera and Wick left Brinegate behind them and rode east along the old white salt road, a pale ribbon packed hard by the wheels of ten thousand carts. Wick sang bad songs to keep the horses cheerful, and Sera, who had never travelled farther than the next village, found that the world was far larger than any map had told her. By noon the wind had begun to carry a faint taste of salt and the distant cry of the gulls.

On the third day the road dipped toward the coast, and Saltmarch opened before them like another world, a vast flat plain of shallow pans that shone white under the sun. Workers moved slowly among them with long wooden rakes, dragging the glittering crystals into low mounds that stretched to the horizon. It was the most beautiful thing Sera had ever seen, and it was strange to think that so much quiet beauty could be threatened by a few lines of ink.

A young salt-raker called Edda, her hands cracked and white with brine, paused beside Sera's horse and explained without being asked that the price of everything had doubled since the iron carts stopped. Rakes, nails, pans and even the bread in her village now cost twice as much, she said, and the families in the huts along the shore were going to bed hungry. She said it without anger, as one states the weather, and that made it worse.

In the next village the market square was half empty, and the stallholders who remained stood with their arms folded and their eyes narrow. Everyone Sera spoke to had the same explanation, which was that the greedy Ash lords were choking the kingdom, and they repeated it with a heat that seemed to have been borrowed from somewhere else. She noticed that none of them could say where they had first heard it.

That night, at a crowded inn with a roaring hearth, an old woman in a blue shawl declared to the whole room that the Ash lords were gathering an army to burn the salt pans. Heads nodded all around the fire, though when Sera gently asked whether anyone had actually seen a soldier from the hills, the room went quiet and the old woman changed the subject. Fear, Sera realised, could travel faster than any horse, and somebody was making very sure that it did.

At sunrise a crier in a scarlet tunic unrolled a long proclamation in the village square and read it out, warning of Ash treachery and calling on everyone to stand behind the Salt Guard. Sera listened with her head tilted, and by the third line she was certain that its stiff, modern phrases belonged to the same author as the false Charter. Whoever was writing the notices, she realised, was also writing the rumours, and doing it with great patience.

By afternoon they descended toward Whitehaven, a harbour town of low whitewashed warehouses where gulls screamed over the quays and the air smelled of brine and tar. It was here that the salt guilds kept their halls, and the guild masters, as Sera knew from the archive, had the power to send every grain of the kingdom's salt wherever they pleased. A tense, watchful quiet hung over the town, like the silence before a quarrel.

Maren Tidewell received them in a long warehouse that smelled of salt and rope, a calm, grey-eyed woman who looked at Sera as though weighing her on one of her own scales. Without ceremony she took a folded letter from her sleeve and laid it on the table, explaining that this was the royal order which had told the guilds to expect a fee on every iron cart. It was the first time Sera had seen one of the false letters with her own eyes.

Sera bent over the letter, which bore Lysa's name at the bottom and a perfect impression of the royal seal, and studied it for a long time with her face almost touching the paper. The writing was fluent and the signature was convincing, yet something in the rhythm of the letters tugged at her memory, like a tune heard from another room. She could not yet say what it was, and a suspicion that cannot be proved is only a feeling.

Maren listened without interrupting while Sera explained about the Charter, and when she had finished she was silent for so long that Wick began to fidget. At last she said that she had run the guilds for eleven years and had never trusted a letter that arrived too conveniently, and that she would hold the guilds back for three days, no more. They shook hands across a pair of salt scales, and the pans swung gently, then settled level.

On the second morning out of Whitehaven they climbed a long ridge above the Greywater, and Sera reined in her horse at the top with a sharp breath. Below them lay the Weigh-Bridge, a narrow arch of old stone across the grey river, and on either bank stood an army, blue cloaks on one side and dark leather on the other. Between them the bridge looked as thin as a thread that somebody was about to cut.

At the very middle of the bridge, an old man in a leather apron sat on a stool beside a great pair of scales, and neither army had managed to persuade him to move. This was Tam Greaves, the keeper of the Weigh-Bridge for forty years, and he told Sera in a dry, cracked voice that he had weighed every cart that crossed since before she was born. A bridge was built for crossing, he said, not for fighting over, and he intended to stay until somebody remembered it.

As the afternoon wore on, shouts began to cross the river, first single insults and then whole choruses, while the soldiers shifted their weight with the restless patience of men told to wait too long. Then a stone flew out of the crowd on the iron side and clattered along the bridge, and in a single heartbeat hands were on sword hilts all along both lines. Nobody moved, and the silence that followed was the most dangerous sound Sera had ever heard.

Before she had decided to do it, Sera had slid from her horse and begun walking along the road toward the bridge, the old Charter held in front of her like a candle. Her knees shook, but her voice, when she stood between the armies, came out clear and steady, asking both sides to wait three days and read the law with her before a single arrow flew. It was, as Wick said afterward, either the bravest or the silliest thing he had ever seen.

Lysa came striding along the bridge in her blue-grey armour, her face pale with anger and fear together, and ordered her little sister to go home before she was hurt. From the far side Lord Kael Ashmoor, a broad, weather-beaten man with a voice like gravel, called out that a girl with a scroll would not stop his iron and that the Halvanes had made enough trouble already. Sera stood very still between them, her heart pounding like a drum, and she did not move an inch.

Sera answered quietly, so that both of them had to stop shouting in order to hear her, that the Charter was the law of both lands and had been the law for sixty years. If they truly wanted a war, she said, they might at least read what they were fighting over first, since it would take only a few minutes and could save a great many lives. For a long moment, on both banks of the river, nobody seemed to breathe at all.

Kael broke the silence with a grunt that might have been a laugh, saying that he had never refused to read anything and would wait three days if Commander Lysa did the same. Lysa gripped the bridge rail until her knuckles whitened, glaring at her sister as though she had been betrayed, and then, with the stiff pride of a soldier giving ground, she stepped forward to read. Sera unrolled the old Charter on the stone parapet and held the corners flat with her hands.

Lysa read the true clause once and then again, her finger following the faded script, and Sera watched the colour drain out of her sister's face as the meaning sank in. When she looked up, her eyes were bright and bewildered, and she whispered that she had never ordered any fee on iron and had no memory of such a thing. It was the voice of an honest person discovering that she had been used.

Without a word, old Tam Greaves rose from his stool, set a lump of iron on one pan of his scales and piled salt on the other, pinch by pinch, until the pans hung perfectly level. It was the oldest ceremony of the border, performed ten thousand times without anyone watching, and now every soldier on both banks watched in silence. Weight for weight, said Tam gruffly, was a promise, and promises are heavier than they look.

Slowly, like a tide turning, the soldiers on both banks lowered their spears and swords and took a pace back from the water, and a long breath of relief ran down the lines. Kael raised one hand to his men and Lysa raised hers, and in the middle of the bridge Sera suddenly felt her legs begin to shake. The three days had begun, and nobody, least of all Sera, knew what she would do with them.

That evening in her command tent, with the lamp turned low, Lysa finally told Sera what she had been too proud to say on the bridge. On the night of the funeral the Chancellor had brought her a thick pile of papers and a pen, speaking so gently of duty and routine that she had signed every page without reading one. Her voice cracked on the last words, for Lysa had never in her life been careless, and she could not forgive herself for being so just once.

Sera sat down beside her sister on the narrow camp bed and, for the first time in years, put an arm around her stiff shoulders. Nobody could blame her for grieving, she said, and anyone with a heart would have done the same, but the only way to put the mistake right was to remember exactly what she had signed. Lysa drew a shaky breath, nodded and wiped her eyes with the back of her glove.

Lysa counted on her fingers what she could remember, which was orders for grain and blankets, new postings for the Salt Guard along the border and a good many pages that she had never even turned over. The Chancellor, she said, had called them routine, and had stood patiently beside her desk with a smile while she signed, handing each page across as soon as the ink was dry. It was, Sera thought grimly, a very efficient way to steal a signature, and it had worked perfectly.

On the far bank, Kael's men made room for Sera at their campfire without being asked, and the lord himself pulled the crumpled letter from his coat and thrust it across the flames. The seal was Lysa's and the words were insulting, but in the firelight Sera saw the same stiff phrases and the same neat, slanting hand that she had found in the false Charter. With Maren's order, she realised, that made three papers written by a single pen, and the pen was nowhere near either army.

Sera drew the others close and showed them what she had seen at last, a tiny curl on the crossbar of the letter t that appeared in the false Charter, in Kael's letter and in Maren's order. Pell had taught her that a hand can disguise its slant and its size but never its small unconscious habits, and this was a habit that somebody had been repeating for days. Kael, who wrote with a heavy scrawl of his own, looked at the little curl with unexpected respect.

A slim young woman in a hooded cloak slipped into the circle of firelight and was introduced as Brenna Ashmoor, Kael's daughter and the best scout in the Ash Hills. She reported in a low, quick voice that a band of strangers in mismatched cloaks, some blue and some black, had burned a barn on an Ash farm three nights before and ridden away unseen. Nobody had been hurt, but the cloaks had been chosen, Brenna said, to be remembered.

Under a swinging lantern, Sera pinned a map to a tent pole and drew lines across it with a stub of charcoal while Lysa and Kael watched in silence.
