If war broke out, she said, the Salt Coast and the Ash Hills would both be ruined, and neither Lysa nor Kael nor the miners nor the rakers would gain anything at all. Only one kind of person profits from a kingdom in chaos, and that is the one who is asked to bring order.

Slowly the two leaders raised their heads and looked at each other across the map, and Sera saw the same dawning thought pass over both faces. Each of them remembered a quiet conversation with Chancellor Karth in which he had remarked, almost in passing, that a kingdom without an heir would need a Protector until one could be found. At the time it had sounded like sensible advice, and now it sounded like a plan.

The first night of the truce passed with a fire burning on each bank of the Greywater and old Tam's lantern glowing in the middle of the bridge like a small yellow star. Sentries on both sides eyed one another across the water, and now and then one of them raised a hand in a stiff, uncertain wave. It was not yet peace, but it was the first silence the border had known in a week.

Deep in the night a rider came galloping down the hill road with a torch streaming sparks behind him and drew rein so hard that his horse slid on the stones. Torren, he gasped, was riding toward the bridge at the head of a company of Ash lords, forty strong and most of them armed, and he had refused to say what he meant to do. Sera felt her stomach tighten, for a truce is a fragile thing, and forty armed lords could break it with one careless word.

Torren rode up to the Weigh-Bridge in the first grey light with forty Ash lords at his back, and every soldier on both banks reached for a weapon. Then, to everyone's astonishment, he swung down from his saddle, told the lords to stay where they were, and walked onto the bridge alone with his head bowed like a boy summoned by a schoolmaster. For the first time anyone could remember, he had not even brought his usual charming smile with him.

In Lysa's tent, with the flap pulled shut, Torren sank to his knees on the rugs and confessed in a voice scraped raw that he owed the moneylender Gilder Prowse a fortune, which he could never have repaid. The Chancellor had paid every coin, he said, quietly and with a smile, and in return had suggested that Torren's famous charm might be used to keep the Ash lords restless and suspicious. He had believed it was only a favour between friends, and he did not look up while he said it.

Lysa's anger broke like a storm, and she shouted that he was a fool, a spendthrift and a traitor who had let a stranger buy his loyalty with a handful of coins. Torren took every word in silence, which was somehow worse than if he had argued, and Sera stepped between them with both hands raised before the shouting could turn into something that could not be forgiven. The old family quarrel had always been kept behind closed doors, and now it was loose in the world.

Lord Kael Ashmoor, who had been standing silently by the tent flap with his arms folded, said drily that now at last he knew who had been pouring oil on his hot-headed lords every night for a month. Torren flinched, but he did not look away, and he answered that every word of it was true and that he was prepared to be punished however the Ash lord saw fit. It was the first honest thing Kael had heard a Halvane say in a long while.

Sera lowered her hands and said in the calm voice she used with frightened scribes that nobody needed punishing tonight, since a quarrel was exactly what the Chancellor wanted. What they needed was somebody who had held the pen, and the only person who could tell them the truth was the clerk who had copied the letters. The three Halvanes looked at one another by lamplight, and for the first time in a long while they were on the same side.

Torren went back to the waiting Ash lords and, for the first time in his life, used his famous charm for something worth doing. Lord Garrow Stane, a red-faced giant with a drawn sword, wanted to teach the Salt Guard a lesson, but Torren spoke to him so gently of tricks and hasty fights that the sword returned to its sheath. It took an hour, and it was a better morning's work than any he had ever done.

With a stick, Sera drew a plan of the palace in the dust outside the tent and explained about the seal-book, the great ledger in which the Chancellor's office had to record every letter that carried the royal seal. If Karth had sealed forged letters, there would be gaps and numbers that did not match, and no clever sentence could explain them away. A book, she told them, cannot be charmed or frightened, and it can never be bribed to remember something different.

Lysa and Kael bent over the map together, which in itself would have astonished anyone who had seen them shout at each other across a river, and agreed on a plan. They would keep the truce at the bridge under Tam Greaves's watchful eye, and when Sera called a Council in the Hall of Two Crowns, they would bring their people to Brinegate. Brenna listened with her chin on her fist, plainly already planning her own part.

In the cold morning mist, four riders prepared to slip away from the bridge before the Chancellor's spies could carry news of them. Sera carried her saddlebags, Torren carried his shame, Wick carried a satchel of bread and Brenna carried her bow, sent by her father to be the eyes of the Ash Hills. They would travel by night and by the back roads, and they would enter Brinegate as quietly as thieves.

Before the riders left, Lysa did something she had not done since Sera was small, and gathered her youngest sister into a hug so fierce that her armour pressed into Sera's ribs. She said into her hair that she had been wrong to think of her all these years as only the little one, and that the kingdom was lucky it had somebody who read before she signed. Sera could not trust herself to answer in words, so she hugged her sister back as hard as she could.

Under a sky crowded with stars, the four riders galloped along the dark river road with the Greywater murmuring beside them and their hooves drumming in the night. Wick led the way, because he knew every bend of the road from a hundred errands, and Brenna rode behind him with her bow across her back, scanning the hedges for anything that moved. Sera, last in the line, kept her eyes on the pale path of the road and tried not to count the hours.

At midnight they rested in a ruined mill beside the river, where Brenna announced that a king's son who could not light a fire had no business riding to a rescue. Torren knelt over the sticks with great seriousness and failed three times, scattering sparks and smoke while Wick laughed until he had to hold his sides. On the fourth attempt a small flame took hold, and Torren looked so astonished and proud that even Brenna's stern face cracked into a grin.

Before dawn they heard hoofbeats, and Brenna pulled them all into a wet ditch beside the road just as a band of riders appeared out of the dark, perhaps twenty in number, wearing cloaks of blue and black thrown together. The men rode loosely and talked loudly, like hired hands rather than soldiers, and they passed so close that Sera could smell the horses. When the sound of them had faded, Brenna whispered that those were the same cloaks that had burned the barn.

At the first grey light, Brenna crept through the bushes to where the riders had camped and lay motionless in the wet grass for a quarter of an hour. She came back muddy and fierce-eyed, reporting that two of the men were grumbling that the Chancellor's silver was late and that they would burn no more barns until they were paid. It was only a scrap of overheard talk, but it fitted itself to everything else like one more piece of a growing puzzle.

As they rode on through the morning, Sera found herself remembering the day her father had first taught her to read the Charter, when she was seven and her feet still dangled from the chair beside his desk. He had put a finger beneath each line and told her gravely that a promise is only as strong as the people who read it, and that most of the wars in history had begun with somebody who did not. She had not understood him then, and she was only beginning to understand him now.

They came in sight of Brinegate as the sun sank behind its towers, and Sera's heart tightened at the sight of the guards in grey cloaks standing at every gate. Travellers were being stopped, questioned and searched, and a line of weary farmers stood waiting with their carts while a bored officer turned over their sacks. It was clear that nobody was meant to enter the capital without the Chancellor knowing.

Wick, who had spent his life slipping through gates with messages that guards would rather not have seen, knew a way in. He bargained with a sleepy fishmonger for the use of his cart, and the four of them lay beneath nets and baskets of silver herring, trying not to breathe, as it rumbled through the river gate. The guard waved them on with one hand over his nose, and Sera had never smelled anything so terrible or been so grateful.

Mother Bessel, the palace cook, a vast woman with flour on her forearms, looked up from a bubbling pot and saw four muddy figures smelling strongly of herring creeping through her kitchen. Two years earlier Sera had found the deed to Bessel's family cottage in a pile of mislabelled papers in the archive, and the cook had never forgotten it. Without asking a single question, she swept them all into the cold pantry, piled sacks of flour in front of the door and told them to be quiet as mice.

At midnight, when the great kitchen had gone quiet and the last footsteps in the corridors had died away, Bessel led them by a back stair to the lower levels of the palace. Sera crept down the final flight with her hand against the cold wall and gave the old signal on the archive door, two slow knocks and one quick one, a code that she and Pell had invented as a joke. This time, as she waited in the darkness for the bolt to slide, it was not a joke at all.

The door opened an inch, then wide, and Master Pell stood there in a nightcap and a long grey dressing gown with a lamp in one hand and a furious Inkwell at his feet. The cat took one look at Brenna, who wore a forest of twigs and a strong smell of fish, and hissed like a kettle. Pell, however, looked at Sera for a long moment, and said in a voice that was not quite steady that he had begun to think he would never see her again.

Pell heaved the great seal-book onto the table, a ledger in which every royal letter had been recorded for forty years, and opened it to the week of the king's death. A neat strip of paper stood in the binding where several pages had been sliced out with a very sharp blade, and the entries on either side referred to letters that no longer existed. Whoever had done it had been careful, but not careful enough to remember that a book has a spine.

Sera traced the columns with her finger, and the pattern came clear almost at once. Each sealed letter had its own number, and across the gap the numbers jumped by dozens, as though forty letters had been sealed in a single night and then wiped from the record. Somebody, it was now plain, had used the royal seal far more often than the book would ever admit.

Torren leaned over her shoulder and tapped a line that the knife had missed, and the colour left his face for the second time that week. It recorded a sealed order to pay a large sum from the privy purse to Gilder Prowse, the moneylender, on the very night that Torren's debts had vanished. He had thought of that night for weeks as a stroke of luck, and now he saw it in black ink as a transaction.

While the others bent over the ledger, Brenna and Wick went scouting through the sleeping palace, moving from shadow to shadow with an ease that would have made a cat jealous. They found the Chancellor's tower dark and unguarded at that hour, with a heavy door below and, beside it, a narrow servants' stair half hidden by a curtain. It led upward to a room that appeared on no plan of the palace.

At the top of the stair, the others joined them in a cramped attic room that smelled of ink, lamp oil and fear, with a slanting desk beneath a skylight and a shelf crowded with quills. It was the workroom of a copyist, and the desk was heaped with practice sheets on which one signature had been written again and again, in every size and slant, until it matched Lysa's own. Torren whistled softly through his teeth, and for once nobody told him to be quiet, because nobody could think of anything to say.

Sera sorted through the sheets by the light of her small lamp and found, beneath the signatures, the false clause of the Charter written out a dozen times, each copy a little cleaner than the last. Further down the pile lay careful drawings of Kael's seal, and in the corner of every page, like a small proud signature of its own, was the tiny curl on the crossbar of the letter t. She folded the best sheets into her jacket and felt, for the first time, that she held something real.

A footstep sounded on the stair, and Brenna snuffed the lamp, but it was too late, for the door swung open and a thin young man with inky fingers stood framed in the light of his own candle. He stared at the strangers and the stolen sheets with his mouth working like a fish, and before Wick could reach him he had dropped the candle and fled down the spiral stair. Wick sprang in pursuit, but the clerk knew the dark stairs better than any of them, and by the time Wick reached the courtyard there was only a swinging gate and the echo of running feet.

They were hurrying back toward the archive when a figure stepped out of the shadows and blocked the corridor, smiling, with two grey-cloaked guards at his shoulders. Chancellor Karth had been told, he said pleasantly, that a party of strangers smelling strongly of herring had entered the palace that evening, and he had hoped to find the Princess Sera among them. She looked tired, he added, and surely it was time she and her companions took some rest.

Sera drew herself up, with Torren, Wick and Brenna ranged behind her, and said clearly that by the old law of Haldmere any Halvane might call the lords of both lands to the Hall of Two Crowns. She called them for dawn, two days hence, with the Ash lords, the salt guilds and the Salt Guard, to decide who should keep the kingdom's peace. The Chancellor considered her for a long moment, and then he smiled and said that it was a most excellent idea.

Karth bowed and wished them a pleasant night, and the guards escorted the little group back to the archive with great courtesy. The door closed behind them, and a moment later they heard the scrape of a heavy key in the lock and the tread of boots settling down to stand watch outside. The Chancellor, it seemed, had agreed to the Council, but he had no intention of letting its caller attend.

Torren hammered on the door until his fists hurt and shouted that he was a Halvane and demanded to be let out, but the only answer was the creak of a guard shifting his weight on the other side. Pell sighed, stroked the cat and observed that in forty years of working in the archive he had never been locked into it, and that it was unexpectedly annoying. Sera, however, was not listening, for she was already looking at the walls with the dreamy intensity of someone remembering a map.

Weeks before, while sorting a chest of old building plans, Sera had spread out the oldest drawing of the palace and noticed a thin line behind the archive's last shelf, marked with the single word stair. She had thought it a mapmaker's error, but now she unrolled the plan on the table beneath the lamp and traced the line to a spot behind the tall shelf of tax records, and her pulse quickened. If the old drawing had told the truth, they were not locked in at all.

Pell, who had known the secret for forty years without a word to anyone, reached up and drew out one fat volume, and with a groan of old iron the whole shelf swung inward like a door. Behind it a narrow stair spiralled upward into blackness, breathing cold, stale air that smelled of centuries. One by one they filled their lamps and climbed, with Inkwell trotting in the lead as though he had walked this way every night of his life.

The stair ended in a trapdoor beneath the open sky, and on the roof stood a little loft of white doves that Pell had kept in secret for thirty years, for nobody reads a letter that flies. By lamplight he wrote three tiny identical notes, summoning Lysa, Kael and Maren to the Hall of Two Crowns at dawn in two days' time, and tied one to the leg of each of three strong doves. They rose into the night in a silent flurry of white, and Sera watched them until she could no longer tell them from the stars.

At the foot of the stair, in the cold dark, the five of them whispered a plan, because the Chancellor's guards could not watch every door. Torren would go to the moneylender Prowse, whose ledger might prove what the seal-book only hinted at, while Wick and Brenna would search the lower town for the frightened clerk who had fled. Sera and Pell would stay hidden in the old stair and prepare the proof.

All the next morning Wick and Brenna worked their way through the crooked lanes of the lower town, asking in taverns, bakeries and laundries after a thin young clerk with inky fingers and a frightened face. Most people only shrugged, because nobody in Brinegate talked to strangers that month, but a young washerwoman remembered that such a man had begged a bed above a chandler's shop and paid with his only good pen. It was not much, but it was a thread, and they followed it down the lane as a hound follows a scent.

Behind the chandler's shop, in a shed that smelled of tallow and old rope, they found him crouched between a barrel of candle-ends and a stack of unsold wicks, hugging his knees. His name, he whispered when Wick sat down beside him, was Hob Fennick, and he had been waiting in terror for three days for somebody to come and arrest him, or worse, to come and silence him. He was perhaps twenty-five, and he looked like a boy who had been crying.

Haltingly, Hob told them how Karth had found him three years before, a poor copyist with a rare gift for imitating hands, and had paid him generously to practise signatures that were never explained. When Hob had at last begun to ask questions, the Chancellor had stopped smiling, and since then he had been afraid every minute. He would tell the truth to anyone who asked, he said, if only somebody could promise that he would not be punished for it.

Wick gave his word, as one honest messenger to another, that Sera would ask the Council for mercy. They bought a porter's coat and a broad hat from a stall, and Brenna rubbed soot on Hob's pale face until he looked like any other tired labourer. Then the three of them walked toward the palace through the morning crowd, a sack of onions on Hob's shoulder, and nobody looked at them twice.

In a narrow counting house smelling of wax and coins, Torren sat across the table from the nervous Gilder Prowse and did something he had never tried before, which was to tell a moneylender the plain truth. He admitted what he had owed, what the Chancellor had paid and what he now believed it had been for, and he asked, without flattery or jokes, for the ledger that recorded the payment. Prowse, who had expected a charming liar and received an honest man, sat silent for a long time before he went to fetch it.

That night, in the narrow shelter of the old stair, Sera lay awake rehearsing her words under her breath until they ceased to mean anything at all. Pell, who was not asleep either, said from the darkness that an argument was only a bridge, and that a bridge made of true planks would carry anybody, however small, across any river. She was still turning the thought over in her mind when something tapped at the trapdoor above.

A soft tapping came from the trapdoor, and when Pell opened it three white doves hopped onto his sleeve with scraps of paper tied to their legs, tired but pleased with themselves. Lysa's note, in her bold square hand, said that she would ride at once, Kael's blunt scrawl promised that the Ash lords would follow, and Maren's said that the salt guilds would come in force. Sera read all three notes twice, and then, to Pell's great alarm, she kissed the nearest dove on its small white head.

At last the sky above the palace paled from black to grey, and the servants, who had prepared the hall for a Council that few of them believed in, swung open the doors of the Hall of Two Crowns. Torches flickered in their brackets along the walls, and on their cushions in the centre the pale Salt Crown and the dark Ash Crown glimmered in the half light, waiting. It was the quietest moment Sera had ever known, as if the whole palace were holding its breath.

By the servants' door at the back, five figures slipped into the hall and kept to the shadows behind the pillars. Wick and Brenna had a shaking Hob Fennick between them, and Torren walked beside the pale Gilder Prowse, who clutched his heavy ledger to his chest as though it might bite. Sera caught Torren's eye across the hall, and he gave her the tiniest of nods, which was worth more than a speech.

A great stir ran through the crowd as Lysa, in her blue-grey armour, and Kael, in his dark leather, strode through the doors side by side, with mud on their boots from a day of hard riding. Behind them marched the officers of the Salt Guard and the lords of the Ash Hills, who had put aside their quarrel, for the moment at least, to see what the youngest Halvane intended. Sera felt tears sting her eyes, and was furious with them, because there was no time at all for crying.

Maren Tidewell arrived soon after, in a white cloak, at the head of twenty guild masters from the Salt Coast, and she nodded to Sera as one nods to a person who has kept a promise. Behind them came merchants, harbour captains, clerks, farmers and mine foremen, a hundred, then two hundred, until it seemed that the whole kingdom had come to look at a girl of seventeen. The great doors were left open, and the overflow of the crowd spread out into the courtyard to wait and whisper.

By sunrise the Hall of Two Crowns was packed from wall to wall, the Salt Guard on one side and the Ash lords on the other, with the guilds and merchants filling the space between like a living bridge. Light fell in long golden bars through the high windows, and the two crowns blazed in it, the pale one like frost and the dark one like polished night. Nobody said a word, and nobody dared to be the first to move, because every face was turned to the Chancellor.

Chancellor Karth entered last, in a coat of black velvet and a smile of perfect serenity, with a dozen grey-cloaked guards behind him. He crossed the long hall without hurry, bowing to a lord here and a guildsman there, and took his place beside the crowns as though the whole gathering had been arranged for his pleasure. Sera, watching from the side with her heart thudding, found that her mouth had gone as dry as old parchment.

Karth spoke first, as Chancellor, in the warm, grave voice that had soothed the court for twenty years, lamenting the sorrows of the border and the greed of certain Ash lords. A kingdom without a king, he observed, was a ship without a captain, and it was his sad duty to offer himself as Protector until the crown could be settled. It was a beautiful speech, and Sera, to her horror, felt part of herself wanting to believe it.

All around the hall, heads began to nod, for fear is tiring and a calm voice that promises to end it is very hard to refuse. Lord Garrow Stane muttered that the Chancellor had a point, and several guild masters exchanged uneasy glances, and the whole room seemed to lean, like grass bending in the wind. Sera understood that if she did not move now, the moment would pass, and so would the kingdom.

Sera walked out into the open space beneath the crowns with the Charter in one hand, the practice sheets in the other and the seal-book under her arm, and her legs were perfectly steady now. She told the hall that she had not come to ask for a crown, only to read aloud what had really been written. Then, in a voice that carried to the farthest pillar, she called for the clerk Hob Fennick.

A murmur ran around the hall as a stooped figure in a porter's coat edged out from behind a pillar and shuffled forward, shaking so badly that Brenna had to steady his elbow. Across the silent floor, the Chancellor's smile did not move, but his eyes became as cold and flat as the surface of a frozen pond. Hob Fennick looked at him once, swallowed hard, and then fixed his eyes on Sera as though she were the only safe place in the hall.

In a thin voice that grew stronger with each sentence, Hob confessed that he had copied the Halvane signatures for three years at the Chancellor's command. He had also altered the clause of the Charter, he said, and had believed it a matter of state until the letters began to start a war. Then he stopped, breathing hard, like a man who has put down a very heavy sack.

The Chancellor raised one white hand and remarked, in the tone of a man sorry to have to say it, that this was only the word of a frightened clerk who would say anything to save his neck. Several lords murmured agreement, and for a dreadful second Sera felt the hall tilt back toward him. Then she said, quite gently, that if Hob were lying he would not mind proving it, and she asked a servant to bring a pen, ink and a small table.

Hob sat at the little table with the whole hall watching him, and his hand, which had trembled on the stair, grew calm the moment he touched the pen. In half a dozen strokes he wrote the name Lysa Halvane, with its proud slanting H, and when Lysa laid her own signature beside it, nobody in the room could say which was which. A gasp rolled through the hall like a wave, and a lord near the front said quietly that he had seen enough.

Sera laid the practice sheets from the attic workroom in a long row on the floor beneath the window, with Kael's insulting letter and Maren's fee order set beside them. She asked them all to look at the crossbar of the letter t, and the lords crowded closer, one by one, until the whole front of the hall was bent over the papers like people looking into a well. The little curl was there on every page, and once seen, it could not be unseen.

Pell raised the true Charter in one hand and the false copy in the other, and in his dry, carrying voice he read the two clauses aloud, one after the other, without any comment. The first promised that iron and salt would be traded weight for weight, with no fee on either side, and the second slipped in a levy as quietly as a thief in a crowd. Nobody needed an explanation, and nobody in the whole vast hall was foolish enough to ask for one.

Gilder Prowse stepped out from behind the pillar, still pale, and set his heavy ledger on the table with a thump that echoed in the silence. He opened it to a marked page and read out a list of payments from the royal privy purse to his counting house, each made on the night that one of Torren's debts was cleared. It was dull, exact and unanswerable, in the way that the truth so often is, and it landed like a stone.

Torren stepped out of the crowd, as pale as paper but perfectly steady, and said in the clear, carrying voice that he had once used for toasts that every word of the moneylender's list was true. The Chancellor had bought him, he said, with his own debts, and he had been fool enough to sell himself cheaply, and he stood before them now so that nobody could say the Halvanes had hidden the shame. It cost him all his pride, and it was the finest thing he had ever done.

One after another, Lysa and Kael stepped forward, each holding a false letter, and admitted that they had been fooled, she by a page she had not read and he by a pride that asked no questions. The hall, which had come ready to blame one side or the other, understood at last that both had been played against each other like pieces on a board. For the first time that morning, in front of the whole silent hall, the Chancellor looked down at the floor.

A roar rose from the hall, first from the guildsmen and then from the Ash lords, until it filled the vault like thunder and demanded that the Chancellor be removed at once. His grey-cloaked guards looked at one another and quietly stepped aside, and Captain Orla Vance of the Salt Guard took his velvet sleeve and told him that a court of both lands would judge him. He went without a word, his back as straight as ever, and only his hands, which shook very slightly, gave him away.

The great doors closed behind him with a boom that rolled from wall to wall, and then there was a silence so complete that Sera could hear the torches hissing. Nobody moved, because nobody quite knew how, after weeks of whispering and fear, to stop. Somewhere in the gallery a baby began to cry, and then, with a rush like a dam breaking, the whole hall began to breathe.

With the Chancellor gone, the question that he had been waiting to answer hung in the air above the crowns, and one by one the faces in the hall turned toward Sera. Lysa stepped forward first, her helmet under her arm, and said in her parade-ground voice that the youngest of the Halvanes had done what neither of her older siblings had managed. Torren, grinning through the tears he did not bother to hide, said that he would be delighted to bow.

Sera looked up at the two crowns, the pale and the dark, and for a moment the wish to touch them was almost as strong as her fear. She was seventeen years old, and she had spent her whole life among papers and shadows, and she knew exactly how much it had cost her father to carry that weight for thirty-one years. A crown, she thought, was a very beautiful way to be alone, and she had no wish to be that lonely.

Kael and Maren Tidewell stood in front of the crowns with their arms folded, an unlikely pair, one broad and rough as a quarry and the other slim and cool as a blade of glass. Neither of them doubted Sera's honesty, they said, but the last month had shown what could happen when everything rested on one family and one seal. They wanted a share of the power, in writing, so that no single Halvane could ever again rule the two lands alone.

At once the hall broke into noise, Ash lords shouting at salt merchants, guild masters waving papers at soldiers, and Pell flapping both arms in the middle of it all like an anxious heron. Lysa wanted the Salt Guard to keep order, Garrow Stane wanted the Ash lords to keep their mines, and half the room wanted whatever the other half did not. For a dizzy moment, Sera saw the peace they had just won fraying at the edges like old cloth.

Sera climbed onto a bench, opened the old Charter to its very last page and read aloud, over the din, a line that nobody in the hall had noticed in sixty years. In the tidy script of the first scribe, it promised that any dispute between the two lands should be weighed at a table of equal seats, where neither side could outvote the other. The noise faded slowly, like a tide going out, as the lords leaned in to listen to a promise older than their quarrel.

Her idea, she said, was not a throne but a table, a Council of Salt and Ash with three seats for the Salt Coast and three for the Ash Hills. A Halvane would sit at its head without a vote, and every decision would be written in the archive for anyone to read, with the Archivist holding no vote but a very sharp pen. At the back of the hall, Pell looked as though he might faint with sheer happiness, and Inkwell, perched on his shoulder, yawned.

Kael bluntly asked what would happen when the Council split three to three, and Maren answered, dry as her own salt, that a level scale only means nobody has yet given the other side a reason. A ripple of laughter ran around the hall, and then, hesitantly, the first hands rose, a salt merchant's beside an Ash foreman's, and then dozens more. Lysa raised hers first of all the Halvanes, and Torren a moment later, and last of all, with a small shaky smile, Sera.

That night the three Halvanes sat together on the palace roof, wrapped in blankets, looking down over the glittering lamps of Brinegate and the dark river beyond. Torren asked, half joking, whether any of them still got the crown, and Sera reminded him that the will's clock was still running, with most of a year and a day to go. Lysa laughed, a real laugh that none of them had heard since their father died, and they all fell silent again, side by side.

Within a week, a great forge was blazing beside the Weigh-Bridge, and as a crowd gathered the smiths of Cindermoor poured molten iron into a huge mould while the glassmakers of Saltmarch waited with white salt-glass. The Council had ordered a new pair of scales, bigger than any the kingdom had seen, to stand over the bridge as a promise that could be seen from a mile away. Heat shimmered above the sand, and the air smelled of fire and the sea.

The work began badly, for the smiths wanted iron arms as thick as a man's waist and the glassmakers wanted pans as delicate as frozen light, and the two crafts shouted at each other all afternoon. It was Edda, the young salt-raker, who solved it, by pointing out that the two things were not rivals but halves of one balance, and that the strongest arms are useless without something fine to carry. They agreed before sunset and shook hands on it, with soot and sand mixing on their palms.

When the finished Scales of Two Crowns were raised on a new stone arch above the Weigh-Bridge, the crowd that had gathered on both banks cheered until the pigeons burst out of the gatehouse eaves. Old Tam Greaves, who had waited forty years for such a thing, climbed a ladder carrying a bag of salt and an iron weight and set them in the two pans, and they hung perfectly level. He climbed down very slowly, wiping his eyes with his sleeve, and told everybody that it was the dust.

The first iron cart rolled across the Weigh-Bridge that afternoon, creaking under its dark bars, while a cart of white salt rumbled toward it from the other bank, and the two drivers met in the middle grinning like schoolboys. Tam weighed each load against the other on the new scales, and the pans swung and settled, and nobody was asked for a single coin. By evening the road to the bridge was a river of wheels flowing in both directions.

As Wick had promised in the shed, the Council voted that Hob Fennick should not be punished but should spend a year making honest copies of the true Charter in his best hand. Within weeks it was nailed to the post in every market square from Brinegate to Pan Harbour, and Sera went to several herself to watch people read it, standing at the back with her hood up. Hob left off the curl on the letter t, and for the first time in years he signed his own name.

In the dark hills of Cindermoor, where the furnaces glowed red against the evening like the eyes of sleeping dragons, Kael showed Sera the ironworks of Ironhold and led her down the first hundred steps of Deepwell mine. She met miners who had never seen a Halvane and families who had cooked on the cold edge of fear all autumn, and she listened to every one of them as patiently as she would have studied an old document. By the end of the week she understood the hills as she had once understood the vault.

In Saltmarch, Maren took Sera out to the pans at sunrise, when the whole plain turned from grey to rose to gold, and explained patiently how the salt was raised, dried and weighed. Edda, who happened to be raking nearby, called out that the price of nails had already fallen by a third and that her mother had baked bread twice that week. Sera, who had read a thousand records of prices in the archive, had never found one that made her so happy.

Over the golden weeks of that autumn, Sera rode back and forth across the Greywater on her grey mare, Pepper, stopping at farms and forges, ferries and fairs, and listening far more than she spoke. Everywhere she went she found the same thing, ordinary people who had been frightened by lies and were relieved to be told the truth. Little by little, the carts, the barges and the bargains began to knit the two lands together again like the stitching of a torn cloak.

The first meeting of the Council of Salt and Ash lasted nine hours, and for most of them somebody was shouting. Lord Garrow Stane complained about the seating, the candles and the speeches, a guild master insisted on reading a thirty-page report, and through it all Pell scribbled steadily in the corner, recording every interruption. At the end of it, nobody had agreed on anything except that they should meet again on the next market day.

Torren sold his fine horses, his velvet coats and the gold clasp his father had given him, and carried every coin to Gilder Prowse with a bow that was almost respectful. Then, to the astonishment of everyone who knew him, he asked the Council for a desk, a pen and a stack of ledgers, and spent the autumn learning how to keep honest accounts. He discovered, with the faint indignation of a man who has been wrong about himself, that he was rather good at numbers.

Winter came early to the coast, and for a few days the great salt pans lay under a thin quilt of snow, white on white, as though Saltmarch had been wiped to a blank page. The Council met in fur coats around a glowing brazier in the Hall, and the Scales of Two Crowns at the bridge wore a fringe of icicles that tinkled when the carts went by. It was, Sera thought, the happiest the kingdom had been in years, and she tried not to notice the dark line of cloud along the horizon.

One grey morning Maren rode to Brinegate through half-frozen mud and stood before the Council, warning that the fishermen of her harbour were hauling every boat high up the beach. A storm was coming off the northern sea, she said, the kind that comes once in a lifetime, and the old sea wall that guarded the pans and the fishing villages was cracked from end to end. If it failed, the pans would be flooded for years and a thousand families would lose their homes.

The Council argued for two days about who should pay for strengthening the wall, and the arguments grew thin and sharp as the sky outside darkened. The salt guilds said they could not afford it, Lord Garrow Stane declared that a sea wall was a Salt Coast problem and none of the Ash Hills' business, and several lords nodded and looked at their boots. Kael said nothing at all, which Sera had learned was the most dangerous thing he did.

Two days later, in the slanting rain of an iron-grey dawn, three hundred Ash miners with stakes, hammers and picks marched into Saltmarch and began driving iron into the crumbling sea wall. They had come, their foreman told a bewildered Maren, because Lord Kael said that iron had always been meant for holding things together. Behind the miners, the grey sea rose and fell like the chest of a sleeper.

Brenna led the second column down the coast road through the sleet, her bow slung across her back, with a long train of mule carts creaking behind her under loads of iron and rope. At every village the people came out of their doors and stared, because nobody on the coast had ever seen the people of the hills walking toward them with anything but suspicion. By the time the column reached the sea wall, it had grown by half again, as fishermen and farmers fell in at its tail.

Lysa did not wait to be asked, but marched the Salt Guard down to the wall in their blue cloaks and set them to carrying stones. By the light of a hundred swinging lanterns, soldiers and miners passed rocks from hand to hand in one long, groaning chain, and somewhere in the night somebody began to sing. By morning it was impossible to tell which cloak belonged to which land, because all of them were the same colour as the mud.

Torren, who could not lift a stone without dropping it on his foot, found a more useful job, riding from village to village on a borrowed mule and begging every cook on the coast for bread and soup. His charm, which had once been spent on flattering lords, now flowed freely at kitchen doors, and by dusk he was ladling hot broth from an enormous pot to six hundred hungry workers. Nobody on the wall, from the oldest miner to the youngest soldier, ever again called him useless, and Lysa told him so herself.

The storm struck at midnight with a howl like a thousand wolves, and the sea rose against the wall in great grey hills that broke into white thunder and flung spray high over the heads of the workers. Lanterns went out, shouts were swallowed by the wind, and for hours the miners and soldiers clung to the stones and to each other, hammering, wedging and praying. The wall shuddered with every wave and every gust, and Sera, watching from the dyke, thought it must surely fall, but it did not.

While the wall held, the water found other ways, and Sera, who had been sent with a lantern to count the sandbags, found a row of huts at the edge of the pans already knee-deep in black water. She waded in and helped Edda's mother and two small brothers out through a window, one at a time, and then, because she could not help herself, went back for the village chest of records, two hundred years old. Edda looked at the wet, ink-stained archivist and said it was the strangest rescue she had ever seen.

At dawn the sea fell back, grey and spent, and the wall was still standing, scarred but whole, with a hundred weary soldiers and miners asleep in heaps on the sacks of salt like children after a fair. Then, over the ridge, came the creak of a heavy cart, and Lord Garrow Stane appeared with a load of timber and a face like a thundercloud, announcing that he had merely happened to have some wood. Nobody had the strength left to laugh, but everybody on that cold grey beach smiled, and Garrow pretended not to notice.

In the spring a late frost crept over the Ash Hills on a still, clear night, and by morning every green shoot on the high farms had turned black and limp, as though a giant had breathed on them. The barley, the oats and the early potatoes were gone, and the farmers, who had hoped to feed the miners and themselves from them, stood in their fields in silence. Grain, which had been cheap at the harvest, began to vanish from the market stalls of Cinderford.

Brenna rode to Brinegate in secret, and told Sera across a kitchen table, with her voice low and her hands wrapped around a mug of Mother Bessel's soup, that the families of Cindermoor were beginning to go hungry. Her father, she said, would sooner eat his own boots than ask the Salt Coast for help, since the Ash lords had never once begged for anything in their history. Sera listened and thought that pride was sometimes the heaviest thing a person could carry.

Sera put the matter before the Council the next morning, not as a plea but as a question of weights, asking what the Salt Coast had in surplus and what the Ash Hills lacked. Maren Tidewell answered at once that the guilds had six warehouses full of salted fish and barrels of preserving salt, and that she would gladly send it up the road, since a hungry customer buys nothing. It was not charity, she added crisply, but plain business, and for the first time that week nobody in the room felt embarrassed.

Within the week a procession of forty wagons creaked out of Whitehaven and turned toward the hills, each one loaded with barrels of salted fish and sacks of salt and drawn by a pair of patient oxen. The drivers sang as they went, a salt-coast song about a sailor and a mermaid with a great many verses, and the spring sunshine turned the muddy road into a ribbon of silver. It was, Wick remarked from the lead wagon, the largest delivery of fish that had ever gone uphill.

Edda, who had never in her life been farther inland than Brinegate, had begged a place on the lead wagon, and spent the journey staring wide-eyed at the rising hills with their wooded folds and dark cave mouths. Brenna rode alongside on her shaggy pony, pointing out the sights, and by the second day the two girls were arguing cheerfully about everything from cooking herrings to whether hills were prettier than the sea. By the time the wagons reached the village square, neither of them could remember who had won, and both agreed that it had been an excellent argument.

In the first stone village of the hills, the wagons were surrounded by a crowd of thin, wary faces that slowly turned into smiles as the lids came off the barrels. A miner's wife with a baby on her hip fished out the first herring with her bare fingers, tasted it, closed her eyes and then insisted, with tears running down her face, that every driver should share her supper. Salt fish and black bread had never tasted so good to anyone who was there that evening.

Lord Kael Ashmoor came down from Ironhold in person, scrubbed and stiff in his best coat, and stood in front of Maren Tidewell in the village square for a long moment, searching for the words. In the end he said gruffly that the Ash Hills owed a debt, and that he preferred to pay in iron, and he had a hundred new ploughshares loaded into the empty wagons, weight for weight. Maren, who rarely smiled, inspected the first one with a professional eye and pronounced it very fine.

One morning in early summer, the walls of Brinegate sprouted fresh notices that claimed the Council was a weak, quarrelsome body formed by the Halvanes to hide their own greed. They said that bread would soon cost twice as much and that Sera meant to take the crown by stealth, in a stiff official style that was beginning to feel horribly familiar. Somebody, it seemed, had not given up, and that somebody had learned patience in the cold school of disappointment.

Sera's answer was the simplest she could think of, which was to throw open the doors of the archive and let anyone in Brinegate who could read, or could find someone who could, come and see for themselves. Every order of the Council was copied into a great new volume called the Open Book, and by noon a queue had formed that stretched around the courtyard. A baker called Marta, who had been convinced that bread would soon cost double, turned the pages with a floury finger, found no such tax and announced it to the whole queue.

It was Hob Fennick, bent over a torn notice with Pell's lens, who named the writer at last, for he recognised the cramped, hurried hand of Dunstan Pike, a copyist who had hoped to grow rich under a Protector. Dunstan was found in a cheap lodging, surrounded by pots of ink, and confessed at once that he had done it out of spite. The Council, mindful of the mercy it had shown another clerk, sentenced him to copy the Open Book for a year, in plain sight, where all could read what he wrote.

In the heat of midsummer a tall ship with sails of blue and gold glided into Pan Harbour, and the fishing boats scattered before it like startled ducks. It had come from Varenna, a rich and distant land across the sea whose merchants were said to count their wealth in warehouses rather than coins. A gangplank was lowered, a red carpet was unrolled across the quay, and a man in a feathered hat stepped ashore as though he owned the harbour.

The envoy, who introduced himself as Casimir Dorne, bowed so low before the three Halvanes that the feather in his hat brushed the floor, and offered the friendship of Varenna in a voice like warm honey. He had only one small request, he added: that he might speak to the Salt Coast and the Ash Hills separately, since their needs, in his experience, were so very different. Sera noted how carefully he had chosen the word separately, and she set it in her mind beside the word Protector.

That evening the envoy invited Torren to dine on board the ship, and over twelve courses of delicate food praised his wit, his charm and his courage in terms so lavish that a less experienced man might have blushed. Between compliments he mentioned, as if by accident, that Varenna would pay handsomely for all the iron of Cindermoor and would be glad to see the hills free of any burdens placed upon them by the Salt Coast. It was a very clever dinner, and it might have worked on the Torren of a year before, but Torren had heard that tune once already.

Torren laughed in all the right places and let himself be flattered with every appearance of delight, while behind his smile a cold voice reminded him that he had been bought like this once already. The envoy, who prided himself on reading men, noticed nothing, and left the table believing that Torren was exactly as foolish as the rumours said. Torren walked back along the quay at midnight and wrote out every word he could remember.

Next morning a convoy of carts rolled up to the Salt Guard's barracks carrying a hundred swords of fine steel from Varenna, each in its own velvet case, with the compliments of the envoy and his masters. Lysa inspected one, tested its balance, admitted that she had never held a finer blade and then said, with perfect politeness, that the Salt Guard accepted gifts only from friends it had known for more than a week. Every sword went back in its case, and the carts went back to the harbour.

A smooth, silent agent of the envoy rode up to Ironhold in the dusk with two guards and a leather bag that clinked, and asked Lord Kael for a private word. He offered twice the market price for every bar of iron the Ash Hills could produce, in secret, on one small condition, which was that none of it should go to the Salt Coast. Behind a curtain in the corner, Brenna listened to every word and tried very hard not to sneeze.

Kael came to the next Council meeting in his heaviest boots, carrying the agent's bag of gold, which he set down on the table with a clunk that made the candles jump. He told them plainly what had been offered and on what condition, and he added that he had never in his life been paid to leave his neighbours hungry and did not intend to start. Then he asked, in a voice like a closing door, that somebody return it to its owner.

The envoy was invited to address the whole Council, and he did so skilfully, praising the Salt Coast for its wealth and the Ash Hills for their strength while hinting that each would do better alone. But every time he praised one land, the other nodded, and every time he tried to set one against the other, somebody laughed. By the end of the afternoon his smile had begun to look like a very expensive hat that did not quite fit.

It was Maren who ended the meeting, sliding a sheet of paper across the table and saying, in the brisk voice she used for buying fish, that the Council would gladly trade with Varenna on the Charter's weights. A treaty written in public, she observed, was a great deal harder to cheat than one whispered in a harbour, and she hoped the envoy would find the terms agreeable. He read it twice and found, rather to his surprise, that he did, and a little of the honey went out of his voice.

The tall ship sailed out of Pan Harbour at sunset, its blue and gold sails burning in the last light, with a treaty signed by both lands in the envoy's cabin. Sera, watching from the quay with Maren at her side, wrote in her notebook that night that a promise is never truly strong until somebody has tried to break it and failed. The Charter, she thought, was a better document now than it had ever been, because it had been tested.

In the long light of summer evenings, Lysa made a habit of leaving her armour at the barracks and sitting on a low stool in the villages of both lands, listening while miners, rakers and carters talked. She had commanded people all her life, and it was a strange new feeling to be taught by them, to be told that the rope on the lift was fraying or that the ferry ran too slowly for market day. The Council grew stronger every time she came back from those evenings with something that she had heard and could use.

Out of the storm and the long nights on the sea wall grew something nobody had planned, a friendly trade in skills between the Salt Guard and the Ash miners. The soldiers learned to shore up a tunnel and to bring a hurt man up a shaft on a rope, while the miners learned to read the tides, tie a sailor's knot and row a boat in a straight line. It was a better kind of exchange, Lysa remarked, than any treaty between generals.

In the heat of high summer, the Court of Both Lands met at the Weigh-Bridge, with the great Scales of Two Crowns gleaming overhead, to hear the case against Dovan Karth. Judge Tamsin Rook, a stern grey-haired woman who had been born in Saltmarch and had married an Ash blacksmith, presided from a plain wooden bench, with six jurors from the Salt Coast and six from the hills. It was agreed that the trial would be held in the open air, so that nobody could say that it had been done in a corner.

Karth, thin and very calm in a plain grey coat that hung loosely on his frame, stood before the court with his hands clasped and refused to say that he was sorry. All he had ever wanted, he told them in the same warm, reasonable voice, was order, and he asked whether anyone present could truly say that they preferred chaos. It was a good question, and it was a measure of how much the kingdom had changed that no one found it persuasive.

Sera gave her evidence last, in a plain dress with her arms full of books, and she did not make a speech, but simply laid each item in front of the judge and read out what was written in it. The seal-book, the practice sheets with their little curl, the ledger and the two Charters were set side by side, and nobody on the benches could say she had exaggerated a thing. The truth, Pell had once told her, needs no decoration, only a very good filing system.

After two days the judge rose and read her verdict from a single sheet of paper, in a voice that did not shake, declaring Dovan Karth guilty of forging the Charter and the royal seal. He was stripped of every office, forbidden ever to hold a seal of state, and banished from Haldmere for life, for bringing two lands to the edge of war with lies. It was a lighter sentence than some had wanted and a heavier one than he had expected.

As the wagon waited at the end of the bridge to carry him to the coast, Karth turned and looked back at Sera and said, quite gently, that she would find the crown heavier than she imagined. Sera answered, just as gently, that she had no intention of wearing one the way he meant, and she watched the wagon roll away through the morning mist until the creaking of its wheels was lost. She noticed, with a small surprise, that her hands were perfectly steady, and that she felt neither triumph nor fear.

That evening Sera walked beside the Greywater with Pell and Inkwell, feeling strangely hollow, as one does after a great effort has ended and left nothing to push against. Pell observed, in his driest voice, that nobody ever cheered a ledger, and that nobody ever would, but that every great and lasting thing in the world was built on exactly such quiet and unglamorous truths. Sera laughed a little, and put her arm through his, and the cat walked ahead like an escort.

Wick was made Chief Courier of the Council, a post that came with a new satchel and a great deal of teasing, and he and Brenna rode the roads of both lands carrying letters bearing two seals. Every letter now travelled straight from the hand that wrote it to the hand that read it, and no clerk in a tower ever opened one on the way. It was the part of the new order that Wick, privately, was most proud of.

A few days later a smuggler with a cart of cheap spices tried to cross the Weigh-Bridge with a set of false weights hidden under a sack of rye, meaning to cheat both lands at once. Tam Greaves took one look at the man's too-friendly smile, set the weights on the great scales and watched them hang crooked, while the crowd that had gathered cheered loudly. It was the first time that anyone had tried to cheat the Scales of Two Crowns, and it was, Tam said happily, the last.

As summer drew to its close, the Weigh-Bridge was decked with flags and ribbons for the first Weigh-Day, a festival that nobody had invented and everybody had somehow agreed to hold. Musicians from both lands played side by side, children weighed feathers against pebbles on little toy scales and argued furiously about the results, and Tam Greaves sold honey cakes at a stall by the gatehouse. It was, Sera thought, the happiest noise that the old stones of the bridge had ever heard in all their years.

On the night before the year and a day came to its end, none of the three Halvanes could sleep, and by midnight each of them had wandered, quite separately, into the Hall of Two Crowns. They found one another standing in the moonlight in front of the cushions, in their nightclothes, looking at the pale crown and the dark one as though they might speak. Lysa broke the silence by saying, in a small voice, that she had no idea what would happen in the morning and found that she did not mind.

At dawn on the last day, a year and a day after the old king's death, the Council gathered in the Hall of Two Crowns, and Master Pell stepped forward holding a sealed envelope. King Edric had placed it in his keeping a week before he died, with instructions that it be opened only when the year and a day were over. Pell broke the seal with a thumbnail, and for once in his life he did not make a joke.

The last clause, Pell read aloud, said that the crown should pass to whomever the people of salt and ash themselves named as the keeper of their peace. One after another the lords and guild masters rose, Kael with his arms folded, Maren with her dry smile, Garrow Stane grumbling that he supposed he must say so too, and each of them named the same person. Lysa said her sister's name the loudest, and Torren, not to be outdone, said it twice.

Beside the crowns, half hidden behind the cushion of the Ash Crown, Sera noticed a small wooden box of the same dark colour as the shadows, and she knew at once that it had been waiting for her. Inside lay a single folded letter, addressed in his tired, familiar handwriting to his youngest daughter, and the seal was his own private one, the small ring he had worn on his left hand for thirty years. Her fingers trembled as she broke the little seal, and for a moment she could not bring herself to read.

Her father wrote that he had suspected Dovan Karth for years, but suspicion was not proof, and a dying king cannot arrest the keeper of his own seal without tearing the kingdom apart. So he had written a will that asked a riddle instead of naming an heir, hoping that one of his children would look for the answer in the records rather than in the sword. He had not been sure which of the three it would be, he admitted, but he had always hoped for the one who read before she signed.

Then came the line that Sera would remember for the rest of her life, written larger than the rest, as though he had pressed harder with his pen. A crown that is given, he wrote, is only a hat, but a crown that is earned is a bridge, and the best rulers use theirs to help other people across. He ended by saying that he was proud of all three of his children, whichever of them was reading this, and Sera pressed the letter to her chest and shut her eyes.

Sera stood before the Council and said that she would accept the rule of the two lands, but she would not wear either crown. She lifted both crowns from their cushions and set them side by side on the long Council table, then drew from her pocket a plain ring made of a twist of iron and a bead of salt-glass. This, she said, was all the crown she would ever need, because it was made of both halves of the kingdom and weighed the same on each side.

The hall erupted into a cheer that began among the guild masters, swept through the Ash lords and the Salt Guard and rolled out through the open doors into the courtyard, where the crowd took it up. Soldiers and miners beat time together on their shields and tools, Lysa laughed aloud, and Torren climbed on a bench and began a speech that nobody could hear. At the back of the hall, Pell wiped his eyes with the end of his sleeve and told Inkwell firmly that he had a cold.

That evening, in the lamplit quiet of the archive, Sera sat down with Master Pell's second-best pen and began to write the first page of a new chronicle, which she titled simply the Book of the Two Lands. Lysa came in first and then Torren, and the three Halvanes sat together among the old documents, saying very little, while outside the Weigh-Bridge scales swung gently in the night breeze. For the first time since the old king died, there was nothing left to quarrel about, and it was a very good silence.
